articles.summary: Egyptian minister rejects Israeli concerns over Sinai railway project  middleeastmonitor.com
articles.full_text:
Egyptian Transport Minister Kamel El-Wazir said on Wednesday that Egypt’s expansion of transport infrastructure in North Sinai and the reopening of railway lines to reconnect the peninsula with the rest of Egypt are part of efforts to develop the area. His remarks came in response to concerns over the projects reported by Hebrew media.
Speaking on Egyptian television on Wednesday evening, El-Wazir said he was focused on restoring the Sinai railway and extending it to Bir al-Abd, then to Al-Arish and later Taba, alongside the Suez Canal tunnels he oversaw while serving as head of the Armed Forces Engineering Authority.
He said the projects aimed to reconnect Sinai with the rest of Egypt, adding: “Why are they upset? Have we attacked anyone? This is our land and we have the right to develop it.”
El-Wazir said a logistics corridor between Al-Arish and Taba would help revive Sinai by linking the ports of Al-Arish on the Mediterranean and Taba on the Red Sea, allowing goods from Arab countries to be transported alongside goods arriving from India and China through the Arab Gulf states.
“What are they worried about? Does the train fire bullets? The train carries passengers or goods and is a development corridor,” he said.
Asked whether Israel feared the Egyptian projects could undermine Israeli plans for an alternative to the Suez Canal by transporting goods by rail, El-Wazir replied: “What is done is done. We are developing our land and this is our right. If this thwarts their plans, they should see what we are doing.”
Israeli reports have expressed concern over the pace of development in Sinai and Egypt’s construction of new transport infrastructure, particularly railway lines, saying it could lead to logistical and demographic changes that strengthen Egypt’s presence along the border.
Israeli platform Natziv Net said the Sinai railway project, which stretches for 500 km to link Egypt’s main logistics hub with the interior of the peninsula and eventually Taba, had raised strategic concerns in Tel Aviv, describing it as a major shift extending beyond civilian infrastructure.

articles.full_text:
The Suez Canal Authority (SCA) is exploring a partnership with Kenyan company Tunasco to develop ports and marine infrastructure in Kenya, as part of a broader push to expand Egyptian maritime expertise into African markets.
SCA Chairman Osama Rabie held talks on Wednesday with Tunasco Chairman Abdul Wali Sharif at the authority’s headquarters in Ismailia, where the two sides discussed establishing a specialised company to carry out port and marine construction projects in Kenya.
The proposed partnership would involve the SCA through its affiliated Timsah Shipbuilding Company and would cover a range of maritime activities, including port development, marine construction, dredging, shipbuilding and training.
Rabie said the authority is seeking to expand beyond the Egyptian market and strengthen its presence in Africa by contributing to major development and infrastructure projects.
“The Suez Canal aspires to open new markets in the African hinterland and to participate seriously in development efforts,” Rabie said.
He added that the SCA is ready to transfer its technical and operational expertise to Kenya and contribute to the development of the country’s maritime infrastructure.
Rabie said the move reflects Egypt’s strategic interest in deepening economic and development partnerships with African countries, particularly in sectors where Egyptian institutions have accumulated extensive technical experience.
For his part, Sharif said Tunasco is seeking close cooperation with the Suez Canal Authority and hopes to benefit from its technical capabilities, skilled workforce and long experience in maritime industries.
He added that the proposed cooperation has received a positive response from the Kenyan government, citing the growing momentum in Egyptian-Kenyan relations over the past five years.
Sharif said meetings are expected to be held with senior Kenyan government officials in the coming period to establish a framework for cooperation and begin practical implementation steps.
The meeting was attended by Abdel-Hakim Zakaria, director of the SCA’s Companies Department; Ahmed Ibrahim, chairman of Timsah Shipbuilding Company; and Ehab Abdel-Fattah and Assem El-Safty, board members of the Kenyan-Egyptian company.
Tunasco is a Kenyan company involved in a range of infrastructure development projects.

articles.title: AGOA Lifeline to 2028 and a China Deal in Motion: Kenya's Two-Track Trade Strategy - Wansom AI
articles.summary: AGOA Lifeline to 2028 and a China Deal in Motion: Kenya's Two-Track Trade Strategy  Wansom AI
articles.full_text:
Summary
- AGOA extended to 31 December 2028: passed by the US Senate on 8 August, signed on 4 September 2026, and welcomed the same day by Trade CS Lee Kinyanjui.
- Same rules: existing eligibility, product coverage and the third-country fabric provision for apparel are retained.
- Retroactive refunds: general customs duties paid on qualifying entries during the lapse after 30 September 2025 can be reclaimed through US Customs, with processing within 90 days. Reciprocal tariffs, fees and interest are excluded.
- Kenya's stake: AGOA apparel exports were worth about Sh60.6 billion in 2024; apparel is about 70% of Kenya's exports to the US, and EPZ apparel firms employ more than 66,000 people.
- China Early Harvest: in force since May 2026, it gives duty-free access to about 98.2% of Chinese tariff lines, alongside China's zero-tariff offer to 53 African countries from 1 May.
- CADEPA next: Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi says Kenya is ready to begin comprehensive negotiations. A full agreement is not yet signed, and Kenya is expected to open its own market in return.
- Trade-law issues: the fragility of unilateral preferences, rules of origin and SPS barriers, EAC Common External Tariff constraints on bilateral concessions, and WTO rules for reciprocal agreements.
AGOA: A Two-Year Lifeline, Finally Signed
What AGOA is: The African Growth and Opportunity Act, enacted by the United States in 2000, grants duty-free access to the US market for more than 6,000 product lines from eligible sub-Saharan African countries. It is a unilateral preference: Washington grants it, sets the eligibility conditions, and can withdraw or let it lapse. Kenya gives nothing in return under AGOA itself.
A turbulent two years:
| Date | Development | 
|---|---|
| 30 September 2025 | AGOA authorisation lapses; Kenyan exports to the US face ordinary duties | 
| 3 February 2026 | President Trump signs a one-year extension to 31 December 2026, applied retroactively | 
| 8 August 2026 | US Senate passes an extension to 31 December 2028 | 
| 13 August 2026 | Trade CS Lee Kinyanjui welcomes the Senate vote | 
| 4 September 2026 | President Trump signs the extension into law; Kinyanjui welcomes it the same day | 
What the extension provides:
| Element | Detail | 
|---|---|
| Duration | Duty-free access for eligible exports to 31 December 2028 | 
| Framework | Existing AGOA framework, eligibility requirements and product coverage retained | 
| Apparel | The third-country fabric provision, which lets AGOA apparel use fabric from outside Africa, continues | 
| Retroactive relief | Refunds of eligible duties paid during the lapse after 30 September 2025, claimed through US Customs and Border Protection and to be processed within 90 days | 
| Scope of refunds | General ad valorem customs duties only, not interest, merchandise processing fees, anti-dumping or countervailing duties, or specialised reciprocal tariffs | 
Kenya's exposure. Apparel is the heart of Kenya's AGOA trade:
- Apparel is about 70% of Kenya's total exports to the US, and more than 70% of its textile and apparel exports go to the US.
- AGOA apparel exports were worth about Sh60.6 billion in 2024, according to Economic Survey figures cited by the Trade Ministry.
- The 43 Export Processing Zone apparel firms employ more than 66,000 Kenyans directly.
- Beyond apparel, AGOA supports duty-free entry for cut flowers, tea, coffee and macadamia nuts.
The limits of the lifeline. AGOA removes ordinary US customs duties on eligible goods. It does not by itself shield Kenyan goods from other US tariff measures, which is why the refund carve-outs matter. The extension also runs out at the end of 2028, so the question of a longer-term, reciprocal arrangement with the US remains open.
Kenya–China: From Early Harvest to a Full Agreement
The framework. CADEPA, the China–Africa Development Economic Partnership Agreement (also called the Agreement on Economic Partnership for Shared Development), is China's model for bilateral economic partnership agreements with African states. Negotiators describe a concluded CADEPA as equivalent to a full free trade agreement. Kenya is among the first African countries to formalise its first stage.
How it unfolded:
| Date | Development | 
|---|---|
| April 2025 | President Ruto's state visit to China; relations elevated to an "All-Weather Comprehensive Strategic Partnership" | 
| 15 January 2026 | Kenya announces conclusion of the Early Harvest Arrangement | 
| March 2026 | Early Harvest Agreement signed; President Ruto describes negotiations on a bilateral deal as finalised | 
| 1 May 2026 | China applies zero tariffs on all tariff lines to 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations; Kenya's Early Harvest takes effect, covering the same lines | 
| 30 September 2026 | Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi says Kenya is ready to begin comprehensive negotiations on all aspects of CADEPA | 
Reading the two statements together. The March remark is best read as referring to the Early Harvest Agreement, an interim, tariff-focused package. On 30 September, Mudavadi described the next stage: comprehensive negotiations covering everything else a full agreement would contain. The broader agreement has not yet been negotiated or signed.
What the Early Harvest gives Kenya. Duty-free access to China for about 98.2% of Chinese tariff lines. Coffee, tea, avocados, macadamia nuts, flowers and horticultural products are among the beneficiaries. According to China's ambassador, Guo Haiyan, avocado oil exports have risen about 700%, coffee exports have nearly doubled, and aquatic products, including sea cucumbers, are up about 350%.
What Kenya offers in return. Unlike AGOA, the arrangement is not one-way. Reports indicate that Kenya will also open its market further to Chinese goods. The scope of Kenya's concessions, and how they sit with its EAC Common External Tariff obligations, are central questions for the comprehensive talks.
The imbalance it aims to address. In 2024, Kenya imported about US$4.3 billion of goods from China, mostly machinery, electronics and vehicles, while exporting about US$197 million, mostly primary commodities. The government's stated aim is to raise export volumes and move Kenyan exports up the value chain.
The Trade-Law Analysis: Two Very Different Instruments
|  | AGOA (United States) | Early Harvest / CADEPA (China) | 
|---|---|---|
| Legal nature | Unilateral US statute granting preferences | Bilateral agreement, moving towards a reciprocal partnership agreement | 
| Who decides | US Congress and the President | Both governments, by negotiation | 
| Reciprocity | None required from Kenya | Kenya also expected to open its market | 
| Duration | Fixed: to 31 December 2028, unless renewed | Interim arrangement pending a comprehensive agreement | 
| Main risk | Lapse, or loss of eligibility after annual review | Scope of Kenya's concessions and their effect on local industry | 
1. The fragility of unilateral preferences
AGOA's value is high, but so is its uncertainty. Eligibility depends on criteria set by US law, including market-economy and rule-of-law conditions and a requirement not to undermine US national security or foreign policy interests, assessed in annual reviews. Congress can let the programme lapse, as it did in 2025, or attach new conditions. AGOA also does not shield Kenyan goods from other US tariff tools, which is why the refund provision excludes specialised reciprocal tariffs. Two years of predictability is valuable, but it is not a long-term guarantee.
2. Rules of origin decide who actually benefits
Preferences only help goods that qualify. For AGOA apparel, the third-country fabric provision is decisive: it lets Kenyan factories use imported fabric, often from Asia, and still qualify. Most non-apparel goods must meet AGOA's value-content rules. Under the China arrangement, Kenyan goods will need to meet China's origin and sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) requirements. For agricultural products, those include market-access protocols and registration with Chinese customs. Zero tariffs do not remove those conditions.
3. The EAC constraint on reciprocal deals
Kenya is part of the EAC Customs Union, with a Common External Tariff applied by all Partner States. That limits how far Kenya can unilaterally cut its own tariffs for Chinese goods. Concessions on the Kenyan side will need to be designed with the CET in mind, through mechanisms the EAC framework allows, or coordinated with Partner States. The same issue arose when Kenya pursued bilateral trade talks with the US. It will be a central legal question in comprehensive CADEPA negotiations.
4. WTO and preference erosion
Under WTO rules, a full reciprocal agreement between Kenya and China would generally need to cover substantially all trade to qualify as a free trade area under GATT Article XXIV, although arrangements among developing countries can also be notified under the more flexible Enabling Clause. Early Harvest arrangements are typically treated as interim steps towards that end. Meanwhile, China's zero-tariff offer to 53 African countries means Kenya's tariff advantage over other African exporters in China is limited. The distinctive value of a Kenyan CADEPA lies in legal certainty, binding commitments and the non-tariff provisions a comprehensive agreement could add.
5. AfCFTA and diversification
The two tracks sit alongside Kenya's African Continental Free Trade Area commitments. Better access to the US and China does not replace regional integration. Firms that build supply chains within Africa may gain under AfCFTA rules of origin while selling into both markets.
What It Means for Each Stakeholder
Apparel manufacturers and EPZ firms
The biggest winners of the AGOA extension. Two years of certainty lets factories accept multi-season orders from US brands, commit to new capacity and keep workforces in place. The third-country fabric provision continues, so current sourcing models

articles.title: Nigeria, Egypt seek stronger economic ties as bilateral trade hits $223m - Tribune Online
articles.summary: Nigeria, Egypt seek stronger economic ties as bilateral trade hits $223m  Tribune Online
articles.full_text:
Nigeria and Egypt are seeking to strengthen their economic ties and expand bilateral trade, which stood at $223m in 2025, as both countries explore new investment opportunities and deeper cooperation.
The Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Sola Enikanolaiye, made this known on Friday at the Ministerial Roundtable on “Trade and Economic Cooperation at the Centre of Pan-African Diplomacy” during the inaugural Africa-Alamein Business Forum (Go63) in New Alamein City, Egypt.
Enikanolaiye said bilateral trade between Nigeria and Egypt remained below its potential, calling for the implementation of agreements reached at the Nigeria-Egypt Business Forum in July 2025 and the proposed establishment of a Joint Investment Council to strengthen economic cooperation.
He also urged African countries to place trade and economic cooperation at the centre of Pan-African diplomacy, stressing that sustainable partnerships could only be achieved when anchored on shared economic interests.
“For too long, we treated trade and diplomacy as separate tracks. Our partnerships endure only when they rest on shared economic interests,” he said, reaffirming that Africa remained the centrepiece of Nigeria’s foreign policy.
The minister highlighted Nigeria’s economic reforms introduced since 2023, including fuel subsidy removal, foreign exchange unification and fiscal strengthening, which he said were aimed at stabilising the economy and improving its competitiveness.
He cited economic growth of 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, a decline in inflation to 15.39 per cent in August, foreign reserves of $54.86bn as of September 24, and a reduction in the Monetary Policy Rate to 23 per cent.
Enikanolaiye also identified the launch of Nigeria’s National Single Window on March 27, 2026, and the implementation of the Nigeria Tax Act on January 1, 2026, which consolidated more than 60 levies, as measures to improve trade facilitation and create a more conducive business environment.
On the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), the minister described the agreement as the continent’s most important trade instrument, noting that 50 countries had ratified it, while 39 were participating in the Guided Trade Initiative.
He said Nigeria had validated its AfCFTA Implementation Strategy, gazetted its tariff concessions, submitted its commitments on trade in services and ratified the Digital Trade Protocol in November 2025.
He further disclosed that a new air cargo corridor established in partnership with Uganda Airlines and the United Nations Development Programme had reduced freight costs by between 50 and 75 per cent.
The minister, however, stressed that effective trade integration required adequate financing, welcoming the roles of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) and the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) in facilitating intra-African trade.
According to him, the Central Bank of Nigeria directed banks to adopt PAPSS from April 2025 to support local-currency settlements and reduce the challenges associated with cross-border transactions.
Enikanolaiye proposed five measures to strengthen trade-led diplomacy across Africa, including making trade facilitation a permanent item on diplomatic engagements, addressing non-tariff barriers and expanding access to trade finance for small and medium-sized enterprises, women and young entrepreneurs.
Other measures, he said, included investing in transport and energy corridors to strengthen regional value chains and ensuring that African countries spoke with one voice during external trade negotiations.
Earlier, Egyptian Prime Minister, Dr Mostafa Madbouly, who declared the forum open, described it as a sustainable platform for dialogue and collaboration among governments, private-sector operators and financial institutions.
Egypt’s Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade, Mohamed Farid, also called for stronger African economic cooperation, particularly in developing an integrated automotive industry capable of strengthening regional production and value chains.
The Africa-Alamein Business Forum, organised by the Egyptian government in partnership with Afreximbank and the African Union Development Agency-NEPAD, is scheduled to run until October 4.
The forum is designed as a permanent biennial platform to translate Africa’s regional integration objectives into concrete investments, stronger economic partnerships and expanded intra-African trade.

articles.title: Opening up opportunities for economic and trade cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Opening up opportunities for economic and trade cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
National Assembly Vice Chairman Nguyen Hong Dien (second from left) holds talks with South African National Assembly Vice Chairwoman Annelie Lotriet. (Photo: Dang Huyen/VNA)
 During his official visit to the Republic of South Africa, on the morning of October 2nd, Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien attended the Vietnam-South Africa Business Forum at the Naspers Centre in Cape Town.
 The meeting was organized in coordination with the Western Cape Province Tourism, Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (Wesgro) to discuss prospects for bilateral economic , trade and investment cooperation.
 According to the VNA correspondent in South Africa, speaking at the meeting, Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien highly appreciated the potential, conditions, and development achievements of South Africa - one of the largest and most developed economies in Africa, playing an important role in the regional economic structure, and serving as a strategic gateway to connect with the entire continent's market.
 In addition, South Africa is known for its abundant natural resources and minerals, advanced financial market, well-developed transportation infrastructure, and strong industrial capacity.
 Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien praised the positive results achieved in the economic and trade sectors between the two countries in recent years. Two-way trade turnover is projected to reach US$1.3 billion in 2025; and over US$1.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026, a 45% increase compared to the same period last year, making South Africa Vietnam's second largest trading partner and largest export market in Africa. Conversely, Vietnam is also South Africa's fifth largest trading partner in the ASEAN region.
 However, Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien argued that while these results are very encouraging, they are still not commensurate with the potential and strengths of each side.
 The two economies are highly complementary: South Africa has strengths in resources, industry, services, finance, and its gateway location to the African market; while Vietnam, as a gateway to ASEAN, possesses strengths in manufacturing, agriculture , technology, electronics, telecommunications, international trade, and experience in developing value chains.
 These are crucial foundations for both sides to not only promote trade cooperation, but also boost investment in high value-added sectors such as processing and manufacturing industries, digital transformation , artificial intelligence, green economy, renewable energy, mining and mineral processing, high-tech agriculture, and supporting industries. These are also the directions already identified within the framework of the Strategic Partnership between the two countries.
 Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien affirmed that the Vietnamese National Assembly and Government are ready to cooperate closely with the National Assembly, Government, and relevant agencies of South Africa to create an effective bridge for the business communities of the two countries.
 Vietnam is committed to continuously improving its institutions and enhancing its implementation capacity in a transparent and stable manner, in line with international commitments. At the same time, it will always share and create favorable conditions, in accordance with the law, to support South African businesses in investing, producing, and operating effectively in Vietnam, because "Your success is also our success."
 At the same time, Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien also requested that South African authorities create similar favorable conditions for Vietnamese businesses when they come to research and explore investment opportunities.
 Speaking at the forum, JP Van der Merwe, Deputy General Director for Investment at Wesgro, introduced the potential and strengths of the Western Cape province.
 Mr. Van der Merwe stated that with a population of 7.6 million, the export-oriented economy of the Western Cape is primarily driven by the service sector (accounting for 70%).
 The province is experiencing strong growth in attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), particularly in the software and information technology sectors. Western Cape is shifting its focus to attracting significant investment from Asia, rather than relying solely on traditional markets.
 Highly appreciating the capabilities of Vietnamese businesses, Mr. JP Van der Merwe considers them a partner offering great opportunities. Currently, Western Cape is importing large volumes of electronic products, textiles, footwear, chemicals, and medical equipment from Vietnam.
 Conversely, the province's main export items to Vietnam are corn, fruits, and flowers. Western Cape expects to continue increasing exports of these key products, along with industrial products such as ships and yachts.
 Wesgro is committed to being a partner and acting as a "center of economic knowledge" to provide maximum support for Vietnamese businesses to successfully integrate into the South African market.
 In an interview with a VNA reporter in South Africa, Mr. JP Van der Merwe stated that, in addition to traditional strengths in agriculture and food, Vietnam's industrial manufacturing sector is increasingly attracting attention.
 Although the number of South African businesses investing in Vietnam is still modest, the trend of expanding into the ASEAN market promises to bring many new opportunities.
 Mr. JP Van der Merwe also pointed out Vietnam's clear competitive advantages, including a market size of 100 million people and impressive economic growth (averaging above 6% over the past five years and reaching approximately 8% last year).
 South African businesses view Vietnam as a key country and an ideal "springboard" for expanding exports and penetrating the vast ASEAN market.
 At the forum, Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Trade Promotion Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), introduced Vietnam's investment and business environment; and affirmed that the Ministry of Industry and Trade is ready to play a bridging role, supporting the business communities of both countries in finding partners.
 Mr. Vu Ba Phu hopes that South African trade promotion agencies, associations, and businesses will participate more deeply in programs in Vietnam, moving towards B2B trade and building long-term cooperative relationships.
 Meanwhile, Mr. Trinh Duc Duy, Deputy Director of the Department of Energy and Oil and Gas (Ministry of Industry and Trade), highly appreciated the role of international cooperation in the energy sector, especially the strategic partnership on coal trade with South Africa.
 Mr. Trinh Duc Duy emphasized that South African coal has always been highly valued by Vietnamese businesses due to its superior quality, making it suitable for blending to optimize efficiency in thermal power plants. He also proposed several solutions to promote business connections and investment opportunities.
 At the conclusion of the forum, businesses from both countries had the opportunity to directly exchange ideas, present suggestions, and receive answers from representatives of management agencies regarding administrative reforms, the investment environment, opportunities for opening direct flights between Vietnam and South Africa, as well as cooperation in the mining and metallurgy sectors.
 Before leaving South Africa to attend the 153rd General Assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU-153), scheduled to take place on October 5th at the Arusha International Convention Centre (AICC) in Arusha, Republic of Tanzania, Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien met with and visited the Vietnamese community in Western Cape Province, South Africa. 
 Dang Huyen - Trung Kien

Kenya's Local Content Bill and the Push to Close Small Trade to Foreigners: A Trade-Law Analysis
President William Ruto recently signaled an intent to reserve small-scale retail and hawking exclusively for Kenyan citizens. While this policy objective aligns with the Local Content Bill, 2025, currently before Parliament, the draft legislation as written focuses on broader mandates for foreign companies. Specifically, the bill proposes that foreign entities source 60% of their goods locally and maintain an 80% Kenyan workforce, with non-compliance carrying severe penalties including Sh100 million fines and potential imprisonment for executives.
Neither the proposed ban on foreign small-scale trade nor the Local Content Bill has been enacted into law. However, the proposals have drawn significant attention due to their potential conflicts with constitutional protections, as well as obligations under East African Community (EAC) and World Trade Organization (WTO) frameworks. Stakeholders ranging from street vendors to multinational corporations are closely monitoring these developments, as any legislative shift in this direction would fundamentally alter the regulatory landscape for foreign investment and trade in Kenya.

articles.title: Port Washington yard expansion that LIRR called a bottleneck enters design - railway.supply
articles.summary: Port Washington yard expansion that LIRR called a bottleneck enters design  railway.supply
articles.full_text:
The MTA has moved the Port Washington LIRR station renewal into design, a project that also extends two nearby yard tracks so the railroad can base more trains there.
The Metropolitan Transportation Authority said on September 28, 2026, that the station and yard project on the Port Washington Branch is now in design. It describes the work as a design-build project. The preliminary design award comes from the MTA’s 2020-2024 Capital Program. Later construction phases are expected to draw on the 2025-2029 Capital Program. The announcement gave no cost, construction schedule or contractor.
MTA Construction & Development President Jamie Torres-Springer said the upgrades are meant to put the station in a state of good repair and to make service on the branch more reliable.
Station works planned at Port Washington
Safety, passenger circulation and accessibility shape the station scope. Ramps, curb cuts, sidewalks and accessible parking will be rebuilt. Inside and out, the station building will get upgrades, including a reconfigured and larger restroom. Its roof and the plaza canopy will be replaced.
New platforms will come with new canopies and a new structure beneath them. An enclosed crossing with new elevators will take the place of the existing pedestrian overpass. Stairs and the ADA ramp will also be renewed. Communication systems and security cameras are due for upgrades, and the lighting will switch to LED.
Two yard tracks for longer trains
The second part of the project lengthens two tracks in the yard near the station. According to the MTA, this will let the LIRR keep longer trains at this end of the branch without getting in the way of maintenance, inspections and car cleaning.
Also in the yard package are rehabilitation of the trainmen’s building, updates to the employee facility and its parking, and improvements at three parking lots: LIRR Yard, South Bayles Avenue and Haven Avenue.
Port Washington Yard capacity since 2022
In September 2022 the LIRR released revised draft timetables for the branch ahead of the Grand Central Madison opening. Catherine Rinaldi, then the railroad’s interim president, named more track capacity at Port Washington Yard as the key to future service increases. She described the long-sought yard project as “the bottleneck to having more service on the branch.” Those drafts still added 10 weekday trains, for 103 a day, without any extra storage space at the yard. In November 2025, MTA Construction & Development told the MTA board’s Capital Program Committee that it was advancing procurement for the Port Washington Station Renewal design, following approval of the 2025-2029 program.

1. Introduction
Ethiopia’s Entry into a Multipolar Global Order is a strategic move amid a tectonic shift underway in the global stage. The world is undergoing transition which according to scholars amounts to a global order change. This notion is apparent, though debatable. The rise of a new model of global governance has been an area where the debate about the unfolding change centered. The South-South-based institutional setup that came into the global fora called BRICS is one of the leading institutions focused on and analyzed in this genre of debates. Pioneered by the rising economic and political powers from the South and Asia, such as China and India; Russia from Europe; South Africa from the African continent; and Brazil from South America, the BRICS was initially established by these founding members of states representing mainly the global south, with the exception of Russia. 
During the last decade, the club has evolved to include more countries from Africa and Asia and has emerged as a formidable setup that demands reforms and changes in the global architecture of economic, social and political development governance, echoing the voices and demands of states and societies from the global south. Ethiopia is a full member state of the bloc, having officially joined alongside Egypt and other new members on January 1, 2024. It constitutes one of the three African nations admitted to the club. Ethiopia is a country playing significant roles in African politics and international relations, and within the traditional multilateral institutional setups of the post-World War II era.
The 18th annual summit of BRICS was held in New Delhi from 12–13 September 2026 under the motto of ‘Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability’ amid an ongoing debate around the crisis of multilateralism and the fate of countries and populations in the global south. During this session, the Prime Minister of Ethiopia presented the country's strategic expectations to the member states. The resulting New Delhi Declaration, encompassing approximately 140 paragraphs, yielded unprecedented diplomatic victories for Addis Ababa. Most notably, the bloc officially backed Ethiopia's World Trade Organization (WTO) accession bid and its candidacy for the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Council. The analysis made on both the primary agendas and policy alignments reveal that BRICS- provides a tangible benefit to member states including Ethiopia. To realize as well as maximize the benefits gained through its membership Ethiopia must navigate certain complexities.
The main agendas for which Ethiopia gained acceptance and support during the 2026 BRICS+ summit are analysed in this policy brief, along with the practical impediments for their realization. This is followed by a policy recommendation to address it. It puts in perspective BRICS+ its establishment and the benefits it delivers to member states like Ethiopia economically, socially, and diplomatically. It raises the questions How can countries like Ethiopia who joined the club recently accrue benefits from the establishment. What are the challenges and complexities that Ethiopia needs to navigate? 
2. The Pursuit of Strategic Autonomy: Drivers of Ethiopia’s BRICS+ Accession
The establishment of the BRICS cooperation framework by the countries from the global south was born out of the growing demand for an alternative mechanism of global economic and development financing that fits to the needs and conditions in this region which find the existing Western-based institutional architecture inadequate. Developing nations portray the Bretton-Woods institutions unwilling to reflect the true distribution of global economic weight (Stuenkel, 2020). Likewise, the frustration of these nations with the existing systems specifically stems from the challenges they face in terms of tied aid, unfavorable conditionalities in development financing, quota-based power distributions in the executive position of core financial and development institutions were some of the areas of complaints (Roberts, Armijo & Katada, 2018). The challenges linked to weaponization of dollar, controversial sanctions and disarray in the SWIFT system utilization arise in the context of a highly competitive global governance landscape, exposing the vulnerabilities of relying solely on western financial architectures (Farrell & Newman, 2019). The fractures in the global order contributed to the rise of new economic coalitions which in turn attracted many nations who seek an alternative source.
The emergence of new alternative sends the signals for countries like Ethiopia which needs to cope with challenges from within and finance its economy and development projects. The growing attractiveness of the BRICS model for many countries in Africa coupled with the challenges the government of Ethiopia faced following the conflict in northern Ethiopia between 2020 and 2022. In the immediate years after the conflict the government of Ethiopia faced several constraints in development financing from western creditors and development financers. This encounter unveiled the vulnerability and the risk of depending only on one partner, making it imperative for the state to look for an alternative partner. Ethiopia’s proposal to join the BRICS should therefore be viewed from the perspective of the pursuit for strategic autonomy. Accordingly for Ethiopia joining BRICS was as a calculated diplomatic hedge designed to expand sovereign maneuvering space and diversify strategic partnerships (IFA, 2026). Viewed from the platform’s vantage point admitting Ethiopia a core African country serves diplomatic ends. As the seat of the AU, ECA, and several institutions of regional importance with the second largest population in Africa Ethiopia brings with it a substantial continental legitimacy to BRICS. In exchange, it sought access to nonconditional infrastructure financing, technology transfers, and an elevated voice in global governance (PSI, 2025).
3. Implications for Ethiopia
3.
1 Navigating Economic Realities and Enhancing Trade SynergiesEthiopia's accession to BRICS+ is a profound diplomatic achievement, granting the country an elevated status in the diplomatic arena of the contemporary international relations the center of power of which is increasingly drifting away to Asia.
Besides this enhanced diplomatic status obtained through membership the economic dividends which Ethiopia aspires to gain are determined by persistent structural realities both within the Ethiopian State and the institutional exigencies of the new framework.
Accordingly for Ethiopia it is imperative to tactfully navigate the intrinsic structural realities of the expanded BRICS+ through the management of   essential internal challenges especially across two crucial axes.
The first constraints would be a potentially delayed or unmet expectations what Ethiopia can get from the modalities of financial bailouts under the BRICS.
The time when Ethiopia applied for membership in 2023 and accepted 2024 was the same year where reportedly the country faced with a depleted foreign reserve and a balance of payment deficit.
The new club could not deliver Ethiopia’s needs of billions of dollars required to bailout the economy under constraints.
On the contrary, the country secured a 3.
4 billion USD bailout from Bretton Woods institution via IMF in July 2024.
Tied to this package the country made reforms in foreign exchange rates through devaluation of birr and negotiate sovereign debt reprofiling under the G20 Common Framework.
Membership in the BRICS did not and cannot replace the disciplinary framework of the Bretton Woods architecture in times of macroeconomic insolvency.
Secondly, the economic relations between Ethiopia and its BRICS partners are fundamentally unbalanced.
Empirical assessments show that the member states of BRICS account for 34.
29% of Ethiopia’s total imports, but absorb only 7.
65% of its exports (IJRISS, 2024).
Ethiopia imports refined fuels, industrial machinery, capital infrastructure goods, and consumer electronics from China, India, and the UAE.
In return, it exports raw agricultural commodities, unprocessed coffee, oilseeds, and pulses.
Without negotiated market access protocols, preferential tariff regimes, and domestic value addition, deepening integration with BRICS risks worsening Ethiopia’s current account deficit and establishing primary-commodity export dependency.

This division identified as revisionism and reformism championed by both the founding members and the second tiers of countries which constitute BRICS+.

Countries in this camp also called the non-aligned states of reformist primarily represented by Brazil, India, South Africa plus UAE.

The nations in this camp are those who have established a significant level of economic and security ties with the western nations of both the United States and Europe.

articles.title: Non-oil Sectors To Lift Nigeria’s GDP Growth To 4.4% – Stanbic IBTC - LEADERSHIP Newspapers
articles.summary: Non-oil Sectors To Lift Nigeria’s GDP Growth To 4.4% – Stanbic IBTC  LEADERSHIP Newspapers
articles.full_text:
Nigeria’s economy is projected to grow by approximately 4.4 per cent in 2026, up from 3.87 per cent recorded in 2025, as stronger performance across the non-oil sectors continues to broaden the country’s growth base, Stanbic IBTC Bank has projected.
The bank said manufacturing, information and communications technology (ICT), trade, real estate, and finance and insurance are expected to be major contributors to the stronger growth outlook, amid sustained improvement in private sector activity.
Head of Equity Research, West Africa, at Stanbic IBTC Bank, Muyiwa Oni, said the strong performance recorded at the end of the third quarter indicated that the economy was gaining momentum, with the bank estimating 4.56 per cent year-on-year GDP growth in Q3 2026.
“The non-oil sector is expected to perform better in 2026 compared to 2025 as more sectors contribute to improvement in GDP growth rate this year,” Oni said.
According to him, the three broad sectors of the economy are expected to record improved performance, with manufacturing projected to receive the biggest boost, partly due to low statistical base effects from 2025.
He added that ICT, trade, real estate, and finance and insurance were likely to remain the biggest drivers of growth in the services sector.
The projection came as the headline Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) rose sharply to 56.4 in September from 54.3 in August, reaching its highest level since February 2022.
The latest PMI reading signalled the most pronounced expansion in private sector activity in more than four years, with new orders and output both increasing at their fastest rates since February 2022.
Stanbic IBTC said the expansion was broad-based, with marked improvements recorded across all four categories monitored in the survey, reflecting stronger customer demand and the introduction of new products.
The bank said the strong private sector performance in the third quarter provided support for expectations of sustained growth in the non-oil economy through the final quarter of the year.
However, the acceleration in economic activity was accompanied by renewed cost pressures, with companies reporting faster increases in input and selling prices during September.
According to the Stanbic IBTC Bank Nigeria PMI report, purchase price inflation accelerated to a three-month high at the end of the third quarter.
Businesses attributed the higher costs largely to increased fuel prices and their impact on transportation, as well as rising prices of animal feed, foodstuffs and other raw materials.
Staff costs also increased at a faster pace as companies sought to cushion employees against higher living costs and provided incentives for workers completing projects on schedule.
The increase in input and labour costs subsequently translated into higher selling prices, with output price inflation reaching its fastest pace since June.
Despite the cost pressures, companies significantly increased their purchasing activity, resulting in the largest accumulation of inventories since the end of 2021.
The report also noted that prompt payments to suppliers helped ensure timely deliveries, while vendor performance improved for the third consecutive month.
Employment increased modestly during the month, although many of the new hires were temporary workers. The additional workforce helped companies manage rising workloads, while backlogs of work declined for the second consecutive month, albeit marginally.
The September PMI performance, Stanbic IBTC said, reinforces the outlook for a broader-based expansion of Nigeria’s economy, with increasing contributions from non-oil sectors expected to support stronger GDP growth in 2026.

articles.title: STAVROS NICOLAOU | How to fully exploit the Brics opportunity - Business Day
articles.summary: STAVROS NICOLAOU | How to fully exploit the Brics opportunity  Business Day
articles.full_text:
Story audio is generated using AI
South African business is entering a more ambitious phase of engagement with Brics, one defined by deal-making, trade facilitation, investment mobilisation and measurable commercial outcomes. More than a decade after establishing the Brics Business Council, the years of building relationships between South African business and some of the world’s largest and fastest-growing economies are beginning to bear fruit.
South Africa’s participation in Brics has created important relationships that should form part of a broader strategy to diversify our economic partnerships. We should not have to choose between markets or regions. We should ask how major economies can expand the range of opportunities available to South African businesses and strengthen our position within global value chains.
The opportunity becomes clearer when we consider the composition of our trade. Our mineral and agricultural resources remain important assets. The opportunity is to use those strengths as a foundation for greater beneficiation, manufacturing, advanced services, innovation and technology-intensive production.
South Africa already has capabilities across automotive manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, agriculture and agro-processing, machinery, financial services, renewable energy, digital services and critical minerals. The task is to connect these capabilities to international markets and investment partnerships while creating the conditions for South African companies to participate further up global value chains.
Our Brics engagement can create opportunities to move beyond traditional buyer-seller arrangements to co-investment, joint ventures, technology partnerships, manufacturing, research and greater integration into value chains.
Attracting investment and identifying export opportunities is only part of the equation. We also need an enabling environment so that South African companies, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs), can participate in these markets.
For an SME, the difference between a market that exists in principle and one that can be accessed commercially can come down to certification requirements, sanitary and phytosanitary standards, customs processes, regulatory uncertainty, access to trade finance, procurement opportunities and the ability to make and receive cross-border payments. These are not peripheral issues. They can determine whether a business enters a market, integrates into a supply chain, or competes for a commercial opportunity.
We should position South Africa not only as a destination for Brics investment but as a platform from which international companies can build partnerships, establish production and access opportunities across Africa
This is where business matchmaking, procurement linkages, supply chain integration and trade finance become important. For Brics engagement to have a wider economic impact, we need practical pathways that enable smaller South African companies to find partners, secure contracts, enter supply chains and expand into other member markets.
The same applies to technology and innovation. Brics co-operation can support partnerships in areas such as AI, digital services, fintech, green hydrogen, pharmaceuticals and critical minerals. The opportunity is not simply to increase trade in these sectors but to develop partnerships that strengthen research, technology transfer, joint manufacturing and advanced capabilities in South Africa.
The Brics Business Council’s evolution to deal-making and trade facilitation is therefore significant. Its objective should be to connect the institutional relationships and policy dialogue built over more than a decade to specific commercial outcomes, whether through investment partnerships, new export markets, technology transfer, procurement opportunities or more integrated supply chains.
The targets emerging from the 2026 Brics Business Forum provide a useful framework for this shift, including the call to identify and address the 10 most significant trade barriers, setting a target to support 100 Brics start-ups each year to expand into other member markets and facilitating 1,000 new cross-border business partnerships.
For South African business the value of these targets will be determined by what they unlock. This is equally important when considering South Africa’s position as a gateway to Africa. The African Continental Free Trade Area provides an opportunity to connect South African production and services to a much larger continental market. We should therefore position South Africa not only as a destination for Brics investment but as a platform from which international companies can build partnerships, establish production and access opportunities across Africa.
That means attracting partners to South Africa to invest alongside local businesses, develop joint ventures, transfer technology and build capabilities that serve both domestic and continental markets. It also means ensuring that market access created through international engagement translates into opportunities for South African producers and service providers.
South Africa’s Brics presidency in 2028 provides an opportunity to shape an agenda around priorities that reflect our economic circumstances and our position within Africa and the wider Global South. That agenda should not be developed only when the presidency arrives. The work must begin now.
- Nicolaou is a member of the South African Brics Business Council

articles.title: Kenya Uses Ruto's Leadership Strengths To Woo Investors In Egypt - The Kenya Times
articles.summary: Kenya Uses Ruto's Leadership Strengths To Woo Investors In Egypt  The Kenya Times
articles.full_text:
Kenya has used the inaugural Alamein Africa Forum in Egypt to promote its trade and investment opportunities, with President William Ruto’s leadership in the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) presented as part of the country’s wider push to deepen economic ties across Africa.
Speaking at the forum, Prime Cabinet Secretary and Cabinet Secretary for Foreign and Diaspora Affairs Musalia Mudavadi said Kenya remained committed to accelerating the implementation of AfCFTA, which he described as an important vehicle for industrialization, investment and economic integration across the continent.
“Through this partnership, and this platform, we strengthen collaboration between African Union institutions and the private sector as key drivers of the AU Agenda 2063. Together we shall shape Africa’s economic trajectory for the next decade,” stated Mudavadi
The forum, held in New Alamein, Egypt, brought together African leaders, government officials, businesses and financial institutions to discuss trade, investment and development opportunities. The inaugural event is being held from October 2 to 4.
Mudavadi Links Ruto’s AfCFTA Role to Kenya’s Trade Agenda
Mudavadi said Kenya’s commitment to AfCFTA was reinforced by Ruto’s role as Chair of the Assembly Committee on AfCFTA Implementation.
The committee is tasked with supporting efforts to advance the implementation of the continental trade agreement and address barriers that limit trade and economic integration among African countries.
Also Read: Full Speech: Ruto’s Lamu Address at the Dangote Refinery Groundbreaking
Ruto has previously called for AfCFTA to move from negotiations to practical implementation, arguing that greater integration of African markets can support industrialization, value addition and trade across the continent.
Mudavadi said the implementation framework provides an opportunity to strengthen regional value chains and create a more favorable environment for investment.
“The establishment of this Committee underscores the significance of African Continental Free Trade Area as a platform for accelerating industrialization, strengthening regional value chains and investment attraction,” Mudavadi said.
He also called for closer cooperation between governments and the private sector to unlock opportunities created by continental economic integration.
According to Mudavadi, stronger regional financial integration would help improve cross-border capital flows and strengthen economic links between African markets.
Kenya Pushes Regional Infrastructure and Digital Payments
Mudavadi added that African countries should invest in infrastructure that can make cross-border trade faster and more efficient.
He called for greater investment in regional transport corridors, cross-border digital payment systems and integrated energy grids, arguing that such infrastructure would help connect markets and support intra-African trade.
He also pointed to the impact of global geopolitical and trade tensions on African economies, saying the continent needed collective economic responses built around partnerships, policies and projects.
“These heightened trade and geopolitical tensions call for collective economic response, with partnerships, policies and projects that translate the vision of Agenda 2063 into tangible economic outcomes,” he said.
Also Read: What Ruto Secured at UNGA as Kenya Lands New AI, Energy and Trade Partnerships
Lamu Refinery Presented as Regional Investment Opportunity
Mudavadi further mentioned the recent groundbreaking of the East Africa Oil Refinery in Lamu as an example of how African-backed investments can support infrastructure development and economic growth across the continent
The project, hosted by Ruto on September 30, brought together African leaders, development institutions and business executives, including Aliko Dangote.
He said the refinery would support the development of the Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia Transport (LAPSSET) Corridor by improving connectivity between Kenya, Ethiopia and South Sudan while creating links to wider African markets.
Mudavadi further urged African countries to develop projects that connect national economies and support trade beyond individual borders.
What is AfCFTA?
The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is a continent-wide trade agreement created by African Union member states to establish a single market for goods and services across Africa.
It is one of the flagship projects of the African Union’s Agenda 2063 development framework and is designed to boost trade among African countries by reducing tariffs and other trade barriers.
AfCFTA brings together the 55 African Union member states, creating the world’s largest free trade area by number of participating countries.
The agreement seeks to make it easier for businesses to trade across borders, attract investment, strengthen regional value chains and support industrial growth across the continent.
The agreement was signed in Kigali, Rwanda, in March 2018, entered into force on May 30, 2019, and officially began trading under its framework on January 1, 2021.

articles.title: Afreximbank, Italy’s SACE to support Egyptian companies’ expansion across Africa: Investment minister - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Afreximbank, Italy’s SACE to support Egyptian companies’ expansion across Africa: Investment minister  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
Egypt’s Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid met with representatives of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) and Italian export credit agency SACE on the sidelines of the Alamein Africa Forum (Go63) to explore ways to enhance financing and export capabilities to support Egyptian companies’ expansion across Africa.
The Alamein-Africa Forum kicked off on Friday and will run until 4 October in New Alamein City, serving as an African business platform to transform the continent’s integration goals into investment, infrastructure, trade and industrial partnerships.
The Egyptian government, the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), and the African Union Development Agency-NEPAD (AUDA-NEPAD) organized the event.
The Investment Ministry discussed cooperation with Afreximbank on opportunities under the Egypt Exports Initiative, which aims to expand the country’s exporter base and improve the competitiveness of local production by linking Egyptian companies to financing and trade opportunities in African markets.
Meanwhile, the meeting with SACE focused on leveraging and developing export credit guarantees and financing tools to support international expansion, as well as exploring cooperation on renewable energy and green transition projects.
SACE is Italy’s state-owned official export credit agency and insurance and finance group. It operates under the Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance, acting as a government-related entity that provides financial guarantees, export credit insurance and risk protection for Italian businesses operating globally.
This comes as Egypt has been taking steps to support local exporters and expand their operations. It recently allocated EGP 6 billion towards outstanding payments owed to exporters under the country’s export support and rebate programme, as part of efforts to develop the export system and provide liquidity to companies. The move is intended to increase export support and promotion each year and open new markets for local products.
Exports are a key pillar of improving the economy’s competitiveness and business climate by maintaining financial stability, enhancing the country’s external position, easing pressure on the balance of payments, and reducing trade and current account deficits.
The Egyptian economy has shown resilience in withstanding pressures amid regional war spillovers, with GDP growth reaching 5.1 percent in FY2025/26 on the back of the ongoing implementation of structural reforms, which provide a supportive and attractive environment for businesses seeking to expand.
The country is also seeking to build an ecosystem that can turn businesses, especially startups, into engines of regional growth, while positioning itself as a launchpad for African companies seeking access to Middle Eastern and global markets.
Moreover, Egypt is pushing for stronger economic cooperation and integration among African countries to unlock the continent’s $3.6 trillion economy, while helping African countries obtain greater value from their resources and expand their role in global trade.
It is worth noting that over the past three years, Afreximbank has provided around $9.5 billion in financing to Egypt across sectors including financial services and approved a $10 billion financing programme to help countries such as Egypt secure essential imports amid regional conflicts that have disrupted supply chains, raised energy shipping costs and increased import bills.
Additionally, Afreximbank and SACE are planning to strengthen partnerships between Egyptian companies and financial institutions to boost firms’ export capabilities, facilitate international market access for their products and support their growth, according to Farid.
This aims to provide solutions tailored to Egyptian companies’ specific requirements and mitigate risks when expanding into foreign markets while also facilitating project financing. This, in turn, will enhance the ability of Egyptian companies to access African markets and capitalize on available trade and investment opportunities.
Afreximbank recently announced a target of increasing its trade-finance disbursements to $40 billion in 2026, from $17.5 billion in 2024, to support regional supply chains and economic integration. Africa is facing a trade-financing gap estimated at $74 billion as of 2025, which can hinder companies’ ability to import production inputs, expand their operations and develop cross-border supply chains.

articles.title: China-Thailand joint port expansion project bolsters Maritime Silk Road connectivity - 巴士的報
articles.summary: China-Thailand joint port expansion project bolsters Maritime Silk Road connectivity  巴士的報
articles.full_text:
Chinese firms are partnering with Thai builders on a new round of port expansion project, the Phase-III expansion work of Laem Chabang Port.
Improved port infrastructure and logistics networks are expected to open up new opportunities for the port to connect with China and global markets and boost Thailand's industrial development, making it an important connectivity node in the country for the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road.
Located in Chonburi Province in eastern Thailand, around 130 km from Bangkok, Laem Chabang Port sits adjacent to the Eastern Economic Corridor, Thailand's manufacturing hub. Every day, huge volumes of containers, automobiles, machinery equipment and agricultural products are shipped from the port to destinations across the globe.
Dozens of kilometers around the port lie multiple large industrial parks, home to clustered manufacturers of automobiles, electronics and machinery.
In the ongoing new round of expansion, Chinese contractors are undertaking Phase-III infrastructure works, including 29 port roads, 16 bridges, a 500‑meter-long coastal berth and supporting container yards.
"Thai‑Chinese cooperation on this construction project is highly important. It helps push forward smooth project delivery and ensures the highest quality and safety standards. Aligned with the Maritime Silk Road initiative, it facilitates Thailand’s trade with the rest of the world. Laem Chabang Port will become a vital hub driving Thailand's trade toward global markets," said Anuson, Thai-side manager for the Chinese-run infrastructure projects.
Upon completion of Phase-III, the port's annual container handling capacity will rise from the current 11 million TEUs to about 18 million TEUs, further strengthening Thailand's logistics capacity linking regional and global markets.
The project has also nurtured a large pool of local engineers and technical personnel.
Pattarapong, a Thai engineer, said the role has brought her steady employment while exposing her to new construction techniques and management practices, building up her hands-on experience in large-scale port construction.
"Local workers account for roughly 70 percent of staff on the ongoing construction site. The Chinese enterprise attaches great importance to creating local jobs and keeps recruiting people from surrounding communities. I am delighted and honored to take part in this project since it is also part of the Maritime Silk Road development," said Pattarapong.
Earlier this year, a new shipping route linking Yantian Port in south China's Shenzhen City, Laem Chabang Port, and Cambodia's Sihanoukville Port was officially launched. It is expected to deepen ties between Thailand and China's Guangdong‑Hong Kong‑Macao Greater Bay Area, and open a fresh cargo import‑export corridor for businesses.
On land, Thailand is pressing ahead with the construction of a railway collection‑and‑distribution system for the port, with plans to boost freight rail links between Laem Chabang Port and northeastern Thailand.
Via maritime shipping lines and overland transport links, Laem Chabang Port connects with Thailand's industrial heartland. As regional transport networks keep improving, the port will further leverage its strengths in combined sea‑and‑land transport.
Over the past 13 years, projects such as this one under the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road have delivered fresh support for connectivity between China and Southeast Asian countries.
The 21st Century Maritime Silk Road is the sea route part of the Belt and Road Initiative proposed by China.

articles.title: Vietnam and South Africa expand opportunities for economic cooperation. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam and South Africa expand opportunities for economic cooperation.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On October 2, 2026, in Cape Town, Republic of South Africa, the Forum on Prospects for Economic, Trade, and Investment Cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa took place with the participation of leaders of the Vietnamese National Assembly, representatives of the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the Vietnamese Embassy in South Africa, the Western Cape Tourism, Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (WESGRO), relevant agencies, and the business communities of both countries.
The forum was one of the activities within the framework of the official visit of the high-level delegation of the Vietnamese National Assembly to Cape Town, the legislative capital of South Africa. Delegates focused on exchanging views on the business environment, trade and investment opportunities, relevant policies and regulations, and areas with significant potential for cooperation.
Integrating Strategic Partnerships into the Economy
In his opening remarks at the Forum, Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien emphasized that over the past 30 years, the friendship and cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa have developed in a substantive and effective manner. The upgrading of relations to a Strategic Partnership in November 2025 opens a new framework for cooperation with a long-term vision and higher demands for quality and effectiveness. Economic, trade, and investment cooperation is one of the important pillars of this framework.
According to the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly, bilateral trade turnover is projected to reach approximately US$1.3 billion in 2025; and over US$1.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026, a 45% increase compared to the same period last year. South Africa is currently Vietnam's second largest trading partner and its largest export market in Africa; while Vietnam is South Africa's fifth largest trading partner in the ASEAN region.
However, these results are still considered to be below the potential and strengths of the two economies, as well as the framework of the Strategic Partnership.
Structurally, the two economies have complementary advantages. South Africa has strengths in resources, industry, services, finance, and its gateway location to the African market. Vietnam has strengths in manufacturing, processing, agriculture , technology, electronics, telecommunications, international trade, and experience in participating in value chains.
Based on that foundation, the two sides can expand cooperation in high value-added areas such as processing and manufacturing industries, digital transformation , artificial intelligence, green economy, renewable energy, mining and mineral processing, high-tech agriculture, and supporting industries.
One of the issues emphasized by Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien is building a favorable legal environment to transform cooperation potential into concrete projects and capital flows. Accordingly, businesses need an investment, production, and business environment with clear, transparent, stable, and predictable regulations; simplified procedures; reduced compliance costs; and guaranteed protection of their legitimate rights and interests.
Trade promotion paves the way for businesses.
From a trade promotion perspective, Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Trade Promotion Department, Ministry of Industry and Trade , introduced the developments in the Vietnamese economy as well as the opportunities that the Vietnamese market can offer to South African businesses.
Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Trade Promotion Department, delivered a speech at the forum.
According to Mr. Vu Ba Phu, in the last five years, the level of integration of the Vietnamese economy into international trade and investment has become increasingly deep and broad. The scale of goods trade increased from approximately US$668.5 billion in 2021 to approximately US$930 billion in 2025. Registered FDI capital in 2025 is expected to reach approximately US$38.42 billion, and implemented capital is projected to reach US$27.62 billion.
These results demonstrate Vietnam's increasing role as a manufacturing and export hub in the region. This also provides a basis for Vietnam and South Africa to explore complementary cooperation models, ranging from raw material and input product supply, deep processing cooperation, and the development of supporting industries to expanding markets for each country's strong products.
The Trade Promotion Agency is ready to act as a bridge, supporting businesses in both countries to explore markets, find partners, and implement specific cooperation opportunities.
International trade promotion programs and events such as Vietnam Expo, Vietnam Foodexpo, VIATT, Vietnam Global International Fair, along with business networking and exchange programs, are presented as channels for South African businesses to gain deeper access to the Vietnamese market.
According to Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Vietnam hopes that South African trade promotion agencies, associations, and businesses will participate more deeply in programs in Vietnam, from exhibitions and B2B trade to finding suppliers and investment partners, and building long-term cooperative relationships.
Conversely, WESGRO states that South Africa is Africa's most industrialized and diversified economy, with a size of $363 billion, a market of 63 million people, and preferential access to African markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The Western Cape province, in particular, has been identified as having potential for cooperation with Vietnamese businesses in the fields of renewable energy, green hydrogen, electric vehicles, battery manufacturing, high-tech agriculture, agricultural product processing, logistics, and information technology services. WESGRO has also built the Cape Trade Portal, connecting more than 2,100 exporters in the region with buyers worldwide.
Energy and business connectivity
One notable topic at the Forum was the prospect of cooperation in the energy sector, including coal trade between Vietnam and South Africa.
Mr. Trinh Duc Duy, Deputy Director of the Department of Energy and Petroleum, Ministry of Industry and Trade, stated that in the orientation of ensuring energy security, serving socio-economic development and implementing energy transition, Vietnam highly appreciates the role of international cooperation in the energy sector.
According to discussions at the Forum, Vietnam's coal import needs remain significant in the coming period, while South Africa has strengths in coal mining and export, and possesses a large-scale infrastructure system to support exports. Both sides could explore expanding cooperation by diversifying supply sources, strengthening business connections, exchanging market information, and gradually exploring the possibility of investment cooperation.
Representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade requested that South Africa facilitate direct contact between Vietnamese businesses and reputable coal suppliers, support access to market information, and conduct surveys and research on investment opportunities in coal mining, processing, and supply in South Africa. This is identified as a complementary area of cooperation, consistent with the requirements for ensuring energy security and diversifying the supply chain.
In addition to policy dialogue, the Forum allocated time for businesses from both countries to exchange information on needs, cooperation opportunities, and practical issues in accessing the market.

By Lebone Rodah Mosima
President Cyril Ramaphosa will participate in the African Union’s 8th Mid-Year Coordination Meeting in Egypt on Sunday as chairperson of the Southern African Development Community, with continental integration, trade and infrastructure on the agenda.
The meeting, to be held in El-Alamein on 4 October, will review progress in implementing the division of labour between the AU, Regional Economic Communities (RECs), Regional Mechanisms (RMs) and member states.
Leaders will also assess implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), the role of the African Union Development Agency-NEPAD in advancing regional integration, and efforts to accelerate water and sanitation infrastructure development.
The Presidency said the meeting would bring together Heads of State and Government of the AU Bureau, chairpersons of the RECs and RMs, heads of AU organs and development partners, including the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa and the African Development Bank.
“The mid-year meeting provides an opportunity for the Chairpersons of Regional Economic Communities to exchange views on the status of continental integration as an important component towards the realisation of the Africa We Want as espoused in Agenda 2063,” the Presidency said.
“The meeting will also assess progress made in the implementation of the Division of Labour between the AU, RECs/Regional Mechanisms (RMs), and Member States.”
The Presidency said the discussions were aimed at ensuring greater synergy and subsidiarity between the AU, regional bodies and member states.
The AU describes the Mid-Year Coordination Meeting as a forum bringing together the continental body, RECs, Regional Mechanisms and member states to coordinate their respective roles in advancing Africa’s integration agenda.
Heads of State and Government are also expected to review AU initiatives aimed at addressing and preventing conflicts across the continent, including efforts to strengthen early-warning mechanisms.
The meeting comes as South Africa seeks to deepen trade and investment ties with Egypt, including through automotive manufacturing and broader industrial cooperation.
South Africa and Egypt on Friday launched the Joint South Africa-Egypt Business Council on the margins of the Alamein-Africa Business Forum.
The Department of Trade, Industry and Competition said the council was intended to create practical commercial partnerships between South African and Egyptian companies while using the two countries as gateways into Southern, North and wider African markets.
It identified mining and minerals, automotive and new-energy mobility, agriculture and agro-processing, engineering and infrastructure, renewable energy and green industrial development as priority areas.
The dtic said bilateral trade between South Africa and Egypt increased by 26% from R3.4 billion in 2024 to R4.3 billion in 2025, while South African exports to Egypt rose 21% from R1.3 billion to R1.6 billion over the same period.
South Africa nevertheless recorded a bilateral trade deficit with Egypt between 2021 and 2025, according to the department.
Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau also participated in the Africa Automotive Investment Forum in El-Alamein on Friday, where South Africa promoted itself as a manufacturing and investment base in an emerging continental automotive value chain.
Tau said African countries needed to move from policy ambitions towards bankable projects and integrated production networks under the AfCFTA.
“We must use this forum to move from ambition to implementation,” Tau said in his address.
He said governments, financiers, original equipment manufacturers and suppliers needed to work together to build projects, integrate African companies into regional value chains and expand automotive manufacturing and investment.
The dtic said investment facilitation discussions had also begun in June 2026 around the possibility of a Complete Knocked Down (CKD) automotive investment in South Africa.
The department said such an investment was now considered possible and could result in job creation and economic growth.
Tau’s discussions in Egypt also included proposals for closer automotive cooperation between the Southern African Customs Union and Egypt.
In his address to the automotive forum, Tau said a possible SACU-Egypt automotive pact could support vehicle assembly, component manufacturing, logistics, technology transfer and investment across regional supply chains.
The Presidency said Sunday’s Mid-Year Coordination Meeting would also provide Ramaphosa with an opportunity to hold bilateral engagements with other African leaders.
Egypt is also hosting a summit of the founders of AUDA-NEPAD on 3 October.
Ramaphosa will be accompanied by International Relations and Cooperation Minister Ronald Lamola, Minister in the Presidency Khumbudzo Ntshavheni and Tau.
