Saturday sees the opening session of the forum, hosted in New Alamein City in the presence of President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi.
Abdelatty’s remarks came as part of his speech during the inauguration session of the forum, where he welcomed the attendees and partners, and express Egypt’s sincere appreciation for their participation in the forum.
The forum is an event hosted by Egypt as part of a series of continental gatherings taking place this year.
Among the attendees are: President of the Republic of Burundi and Chairperson of the African Union Évariste Ndayishimiye; Chairperson of the African Union Commission Mr. Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, CEO of the African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD) Ms. Nardos Bekele-Thomas; Dr. George Elombi, Executive Vice President of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank).
“We meet today to launch a new platform for African economic dialogue, bringing together governments, continental institutions, the business community, the private sector, and financial and development institutions,” FM Badr Abdelatty said in his speech.
He added that this initiative is driven by the firm conviction that economic integration is not built through decisions alone, but rather through partnerships that transform those decisions into tangible investments, projects, and opportunities.
The launch of this forum serves to implement African Union Decision No. 973—adopted during the February 2026 summit in Addis Ababa—which mandates holding this event biennially in the city of Alamein.
Organized in collaboration with the African Union Commission, the African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD), and the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), the forum reflects a shared aspiration to advance the mechanisms of African economic cooperation and to bolster the private sector's role in the continent's integration and development journey, he explained.
He continued saying: “Ladies and gentlemen, placing the business community and the private sector at the heart of this forum is no coincidence.”
The private sector is a primary engine for growth and job creation across the continent, he said, adding that the private sector is also an indispensable partner in boosting trade and investment, building value chains, and enhancing the competitiveness of African economies.
Accordingly, the forum’s program is designed to integrate political vision, institutional expertise, and the practical capabilities of the business community.
FM Abdelatty went on saying that this forum “serves as a unique platform bringing together diverse stakeholders dedicated to advancing investment, trade, and development across the continent.”
Among those partners he mentioned are governments, business community, private sector, capable of translating existing political will into tangible projects and partnerships while fostering South-South cooperation. Also included are international and African financial institutions and funding bodies responsible for providing the requisite financing mechanisms and facilities.
Consequently, the forum provides an inclusive space where these efforts converge and complement one another.
Abdelatty, in his words, highlighted that Africa is not merely a continent of raw materials, but a continent with human and material potential capable of building productive economies and achieving development across various fields.
He further mentioned the Julius Nyerere Dam project in Tanzania as a prominent testament to what the continent can achieve when its capabilities and potential are integrated and the necessary political will is present.
“Your Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, our gathering today marks the beginning of a journey that we hope will evolve with each successive edition. We envision this forum becoming a regular platform connecting decision-makers with the business community and financial institutions—a space for identifying opportunities, forging partnerships, and following up on agreed-upon initiatives,” he said.
“In this context, I extend my sincere thanks and appreciation to His Excellency President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi for his belief in the concept of creating this pan-African platform for high-level dialogue between business and political leaders across the continent, and for personally overcoming all obstacles to convene it in such record time.”
I also acknowledge his successful efforts to transform the city of El Alamein—long associated with the remnants of landmines—into a modern, advanced city and a global tourist destination attracting visitors from around the world.
Abdelatty also thanked all Egypt’s partners, including African and international states and institutions, as well as representatives from the private sector and financial, international, and development organizations—for their contributions to the success of this initiative.
“I wish you fruitful deliberations and look forward to welcoming you to the second edition of the forum in the beautiful city of New Alamein in 2028. Thank you very much,: he concluded.

The Vietnam-South Africa Economic, Trade, and Investment Cooperation Prospects Forum, held in Cape Town (Republic of South Africa) on October 2, 2026, opened a space for practical exchanges between management agencies, trade promotion organizations, and business communities of the two countries, aiming to concretize cooperation potential within the framework of the Strategic Partnership.
According to information from the Trade Promotion Agency, on October 2, 2026, a forum on prospects for economic, trade, and investment cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa took place in Cape Town, Republic of South Africa . The forum was attended by leaders of the Vietnamese National Assembly, representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade , the Vietnamese Embassy in South Africa, the Western Cape Tourism, Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (WESGRO), relevant agencies, and the business communities of both countries.
The forum is one of the important activities within the framework of the official visit of the high-level delegation of the Vietnamese National Assembly to Cape Town, the legislative capital of South Africa.
The forum focused on exchanging views on the business environment, trade and investment opportunities, relevant policies and regulations, and discussing areas with potential for extensive cooperation in the future.
Deepening the Strategic Partnership into an economic one.
In his opening remarks at the Forum, Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien emphasized that over the past 30 years, the friendship and cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa have developed in a substantive and effective manner. The upgrading of relations to a Strategic Partnership in November 2025 opens a new framework for cooperation with a long-term vision and higher demands for quality and effectiveness. Economic, trade, and investment cooperation is identified as one of the important pillars.
According to the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly, bilateral trade turnover is projected to reach approximately US$1.3 billion in 2025; and over US$1.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026, a 45% increase compared to the same period last year. South Africa is currently Vietnam's second largest trading partner and its largest export market in Africa; while Vietnam is South Africa's fifth largest trading partner in the ASEAN region.
However, the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly stated that these results are still not commensurate with the potential and strengths of the two economies, as well as the Strategic Partnership between the two countries.
The two economies complement each other in many ways. South Africa has strengths in resources, industry, services, finance, and its gateway location to the African market; while Vietnam has strengths in manufacturing, processing, agriculture , technology, electronics, telecommunications, international trade, and experience in participating in value chains.
Based on that foundation, the two sides can expand cooperation in high value-added areas such as processing and manufacturing industries, digital transformation , artificial intelligence, green economy, renewable energy, mining and mineral processing, high-tech agriculture, and supporting industries.
In particular, the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly emphasized the need to build a favorable legal environment to transform cooperation potential into concrete projects and capital flows: "Businesses need an investment and business environment where regulations are clear, transparent, stable, and predictable; procedures are simplified; compliance costs are minimized; and legitimate rights and interests are guaranteed."
The Vice Chairman of the National Assembly affirmed that the Vietnamese National Assembly and Government are ready to cooperate with the National Assembly, Government, and relevant agencies of South Africa to create an effective bridge for the business communities of the two countries.
For his part, JP van der Merwe, Deputy Director for Investment at the Western Cape Tourism, Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (WESGRO), South Africa, stated that South Africa is the most industrialized and diversified economy in Africa, with a size of $363 billion, a market of 63 million people, preferential access to African markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), and is home to approximately half of the multinational corporations operating in Africa.
WESGRO recognizes that the Western Cape region of South Africa has significant potential for cooperation with Vietnamese businesses in areas such as renewable energy, green hydrogen, electric vehicles, battery manufacturing, high-tech agriculture, agricultural product processing, logistics, and information technology services. To support investors and importers, the agency has developed the Cape Trade Portal, connecting over 2,100 exporters in the region with buyers worldwide.

Trade promotion - A bridge to realize cooperation opportunities.
From a trade promotion perspective, Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Trade Promotion Department, Ministry of Industry and Trade, introduced the positive developments in the Vietnamese economy as well as the opportunities that the Vietnamese market can offer to South African businesses.
According to Mr. Vu Ba Phu, in the last five years, the level of integration of the Vietnamese economy into international trade and investment has become increasingly deep and broad. The scale of goods trade increased from approximately US$668.5 billion in 2021 to approximately US$930 billion in 2025. Along with this, Vietnam continues to maintain its ability to attract foreign investment, with registered FDI capital reaching approximately US$38.42 billion in 2025 and implemented capital reaching US$27.62 billion.
These results show that Vietnam is not only a consumer market but is increasingly becoming a production and export hub in the region.
For South Africa, this provides a basis for both sides to study complementary cooperation models, ranging from supplying raw materials and inputs, cooperating in deep processing, developing supporting industries, to expanding markets for products in which each country has a competitive advantage.
Director Vu Ba Phu affirmed that the Trade Promotion Department is ready to play a bridging role, supporting businesses of both countries in understanding markets, finding partners, and implementing specific cooperation opportunities.
International trade promotion programs and events such as Vietnam Expo, Vietnam Foodexpo, VIATT, Vietnam Global International Fair, along with business networking and exchange programs, are presented as practical channels for South African businesses to gain deeper access to the Vietnamese market.
“ We hope to invite South African trade promotion agencies, associations, and businesses to participate more deeply in programs in Vietnam, not only as visitors but also to participate in exhibitions, B2B trade, supplier search, investment partner search, and building long-term cooperative relationships, ” said Mr. Vu Ba Phu.
Therefore, the Trade Promotion Department proposed strengthening market information exchange, connecting businesses by industry, building regular cooperation programs between associations and trade promotion organizations, and increasing two-way business delegations to survey markets and seek investment opportunities.
Strengthening cooperation in the energy sector, including coal trade.
A notable topic at the Forum was the discussion on prospects for cooperation in the energy sector, including coal trade, between Vietnam and South Africa.
According to Mr. Trinh Duc Duy, Deputy Director of the Department of Energy and Petroleum, Ministry of Industry and Trade, in its orientation to ensure energy security, serve socio-economic development and implement energy transition, Vietnam highly appreciates the role of international cooperation in the energy sector.
According to discussions at the Forum, Vietnam's coal import needs will remain significant in the coming period, while South Africa has strengths in coal mining and exporting, and possesses a large-scale infrastructure system to support exports.
Therefore, both sides can explore expanding cooperation by diversifying supply sources, strengthening business connections, exchanging market information, and gradually researching the possibility of investment cooperation.

This is considered a complementary approach to cooperation, consistent with the requirements for ensuring energy security and diversifying the supply chain.

articles.title: How has Peru’s export-led economic boom survived political chaos? - Dialogue Earth
articles.summary: How has Peru’s export-led economic boom survived political chaos?  Dialogue Earth
articles.full_text:
In the early 2000s, Herbert Vilcapoma saw a business opportunity in Peru’s mining industry. Having learned the trade while working at a drilling equipment factory, he took out a loan and founded Rock Drill. His company now provides drilling services to some of the country’s largest mining companies.
Since he embarked on this venture, Peru has transitioned from authoritarianism to a democracy marked by instability: nine presidents in the past decade, the temporary dissolution of congress, a failed coup, protests leaving dozens dead, former presidents investigated for corruption, and near-constant confrontation between congress and the executive branch.
In late July, Keiko Fujimori, the daughter of ex-president Alberto Fujimori (1990-2000), was sworn in as president. Her narrow victory of fewer than 50,000 votes marked the return to power of one of Peru’s most controversial political dynasties.
The Peruvian economy, however, has followed the opposite trajectory. GDP has maintained uninterrupted growth (3.4% in 2025) while the sol consolidated its position as one of the region’s most stable currencies.
Vilcapoma now chairs VILBRA Group, a conglomerate of Rock Drill and three other mining companies. He tells Dialogue Earth that Peruvian entrepreneurs “continue to bet on the country because of the favourable economic conditions”.
With so much political turbulence, how has the Peruvian economy managed to survive?
Macroeconomic discipline
One of the main factors behind this resilience has been economic discipline, underpinned by inflation control and the stability of the sol. The central reserve bank of Peru (BCRP) is responsible for this task. Peru’s constitution of 1993 guarantees the bank autonomy to conduct monetary policy independently of the government, although the BCRP’s board members are appointed by the senate and the executive. Since 2007 it has targeted inflation of 1-3%, in a region where bouts of three-digit inflation rates are not uncommon.
“Thanks to the BCRP’s autonomy, Peru has recorded one of the lowest inflation rates in Latin America, and even in the world, over the past two decades,” Peru’s former economics minister Waldo Mendoza tells Dialogue Earth. In 2025, Peru recorded annual inflation of 1.51%, while the region’s major economies – Brazil, Mexico, Chile and Uruguay – all hit 3.5% or more.
As the presidency has chopped and changed, BCRP leadership has remained stable, headed by Julio Velarde since 2006. Fujimori has chosen to retain him at the helm for her five-year term.
The Economics and Finance Ministry (MEF) has also sought to keep public spending and debt under control. In June the fiscal deficit fell to 1.3% of GDP, below the 1.8% target set for 2026. Public debt remains at around 29% of GDP, one of the lowest levels in the region.
An export boom intertwined with China
In 2000, Peru’s exports were at approximately USD 6.3 billion. This year, that figure could exceed USD 118 billion. That growth has been driven by more than 20 free trade agreements, which now connect Peruvian companies with some of the world’s largest markets.
“We went from having a market of 34 million people to billions,” Julio Pérez, former president of the Peruvian Association of Exporters (ADEX), tells Dialogue Earth.
According to Hugo Perea, chief economist for Peru at the banking think-tank BBVA Research, the inflow of foreign currency has boosted international reserves, helped stabilise the exchange rate and reduced the economy’s vulnerability to periods of turbulence.
Mining has been the main driver of this inflow. Copper and gold, along with zinc, silver and other minerals, account for around 70% of all Peruvian exports. According to US Geological Survey data, only Chile and the Democratic Republic of Congo produce more copper than Peru – a trend set to continue. Copper demand is being supercharged by its critical role in the global energy transition as a building block in many renewable energy technologies.
In recent years, the boom in metal prices has strengthened Peru’s mining momentum and consolidated its position as the country’s main source of foreign currency, explains Víctor Gobitz, CEO of the Lima-based copper miner Quilla Resources. “It is estimated that for every formal job, the mining industry generates eight indirect jobs,” he adds.
This has been supplemented by the rapid expansion of agricultural exports which, for 2026, were approaching USD 7 billion by the middle of September.
China has been crucial to these expansions. Since 2014, it has displaced the US as Peru’s main trading partner, driven by its growing need for copper, iron and other minerals. In the first half of 2026, the US accounted for 9.3% of Peruvian exports, China for 38.6%. Peruvian blueberries, grapes and avocados have also gained ground, now ranking among its five leading agricultural exports to China.
This relationship extends far beyond trade. According to estimates by the San Marcos Centre for Asian Studies (CEAS) in Lima, China is behind 25% of all foreign investment in Peru – the largest share. In Latin America, only Brazil receives more Chinese capital.
That presence extends into strategic sectors such as mining, energy, infrastructure and logistics. Chinese companies control key assets such as Las Bambas, one of the world’s largest copper mines, as well as electricity distribution networks in Lima, following the acquisition of energy company Enel by the state-owned China Southern Power Grid International.
Seventy kilometres north of Lima, the Chancay megaport is among the most notable examples. It received more than USD 3.5 billion in Chinese investment, one of the largest investments in Latin America under China’s Belt and Road Initiative.
Persistent fiscal gaps
Nearly 25 years after founding Rock Drill, Vilcapoma says his companies employ more than 1,600 people, and a facility is being prepared that will double production capacity.
But Peru’s macroeconomic growth has not translated into improved living standards for everyone. Dialogue Earth consulted the economist José de Echave, a mining and environmental issues researcher from the Peruvian human rights and environmental justice NGO CooperAcción: “Growth has not been inclusive, nor has it generated greater wellbeing for the population as a whole.”
Wealth remains unevenly distributed. Poverty fell from 27.6% to 25.7% between 2024 and 2025, but remains above pre-2019 levels: as of 2025, there were 2.3 million more Peruvians living in poverty than before the Covid-19 pandemic began in 2020, despite increased private investment.
Seven out of 10 Peruvians work in the informal economy, which means they lack access to benefits such as health insurance and pension contributions. There are also major gaps in basic services: only 37.5% of Peruvians had access to safely managed drinking water services according to a 2024 government report; access to healthcare and education remains marked by deep inequalities.
This social challenge comes as the country’s economic stability faces new risks. While Peru retains fiscal strengths, public finances have deteriorated over the past five years as politicians of all stripes have made spending pledges without clear funding plans.
Growth has not been inclusive, nor has it generated greater wellbeing for the population as a whole
José de Echave, researcher at CooperAcción
Dialogue Earth consulted Carolina Trivelli, a member of the economics and finance ministry’s Fiscal Council. This body is responsible for monitoring the sustainability of public finances in Peru. Trivelli points to several measures approved by congress between 2021 and June 2026: according to data issued by congress and analysed by the Fiscal Council, a total of 258 laws that will increase public spending have been approved. Of these, the 48 passed since September 2025 would generate an estimated permanent annual fiscal cost of USD 6.9 billion – 1.9% of GDP. Among them is an increase in teachers’ pensions, which would entail annual spending of USD 2.4 billion.
At the same time, congress has been approving tax exemptions. Responding to the release of the government’s 2026-2029 macroeconomic framework that underpins the public sector budget, the Fiscal Council criticised these tax cuts. In its opinion of a draft version of the framework, the council underlined the need for “measures aimed at increasing permanent tax revenues” and limiting “new tax benefits that erode the tax base”. Pointing to concerns over the tax implications of recent government policies, the opinion advised the economics and finance ministry to “conduct a comprehensive, transparent, and up-to-date assessment of the current tax situation”.
Critics of these policies say they are populist, because they seek to address social gaps while also reducing government revenues, without adequate technical support or a clear source of financing.
“We would love to solve all of the country’s problems, but if we commit the state’s resources for the next 30, 40 or 50 years without backing them with sound public policies, at some point the state will collapse,” says Echave.
“As long as the state has sufficient resources, the problem will probably not be apparent,” Trivelli tells Dialogue Earth. “But when revenues decline and the current favourable cycle for minerals moderates, that is when the real problem will emerge.”
Trivelli considers the recent ruling by Peru’s constitutional court to be a first step towards restoring fiscal discipline. It once again limits the ability of congress to pass laws that entail new government spending. It also requires any parliamentary initiative that increases expenditure to identify a source of funding.
President Fujimori acknowledged this challenge in her first State of the Nation address by naming fiscal sustainability among her priorities: “We will put public finances in order, eliminate unnecessary spending and use every sol of public money responsibly.”

articles.full_text:
The EU–Tanzania roadshow continued in Cesena on 1 October, opening the Italian leg with investment pitches in agro-processing, renewable energy and digital infrastructure.
Tanzania highlighted projects in rice, cashew and coffee, alongside power generation, transmission and digital connectivity.
The Cesena meetings were the fourth day of the EU–Tanzania Investment and Business Forum 2026–2027 roadshows, following two days in Helsinki.
The programme at Cesena Fiera began with an opening session, followed by presentations from Tanzania’s investment promotion agencies and breakout sessions on agribusiness, digital transformation, and renewable energy and power.
Marc Stalmans, Head of Cooperation at the EU Delegation to Tanzania, described the roadshow as a way to bring European companies closer to Tanzanian opportunities before the main business forum.
He outlined Tanzania’s Vision 2050 ambition to quadruple GDP per capita over 25 years, its natural resources and the limited presence of EU companies.
Agriculture, mining, transport, renewable energy and digital infrastructure were among sectors with scope to expand, alongside critical minerals such as graphite, nickel, copper, lithium and cobalt.
The EU offers grants, guarantees, blended finance and loans through European development finance institutions.
Stalmans referred to a EUR 156 million grant package for Tanzania approved at the end of July, describing it as part of a renewed economic partnership.
The EU–Tanzania Investment and Business Forum is tentatively scheduled for 2027 in Dar es Salaam.
Deputy Minister Sets Out Tanzania’s Investment Case for Italian Companies
The Deputy Minister of State in the President’s Office for Planning and Investment, Hon. Dr. Pius Stephen Chaya, framed Tanzania’s investment offer around a shift from exporting raw commodities to processing and exporting higher-value products.
He urged Italian companies to invest across agricultural value chains, from production and storage to processing, packaging, cold-chain logistics and market access.
An Italian Trade Agency study valued Tanzania’s packaging market at about USD 370 million in 2024, pointing to demand for Italian food-processing and packaging machinery, refrigeration, bottling, labelling and quality-control systems.
Chaya also outlined opportunities in precision farming, smart irrigation, digital market platforms, weather information, traceability, digital payments and supply-chain management, and invited Italian financial institutions to develop buyer-credit frameworks.
Investors can use Tanzania as a base to serve the East African Community, the Southern African Development Community and the African Continental Free Trade Area, with support from the President’s Office for Planning and Investment, the Tanzania Investment and Special Economic Zones Authority (TISEZA) and the Zanzibar Investment Promotion Authority (ZIPA) throughout the investment cycle.
He identified local value addition, jobs, technology transfer, skills, export growth and links with local enterprises as priorities.
“Come not only to sell to Tanzania, but to produce, process, innovate, as well as export from Tanzania,” he urged.
On energy, Chaya welcomed Italian expertise in renewable generation, storage, transmission and distribution, naming solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal and biomass.
He also highlighted decentralized opportunities in mini-grids, rural solar, clean cooking and productive use of energy in agriculture and manufacturing, linking the sector to Italy’s Mattei Plan for Africa.
In digital infrastructure, he cited broadband, data centres, cloud services, cybersecurity, fintech, e-government, artificial intelligence and digital skills, and recalled 2024 discussions between Tanzania and Sparkle on ICT infrastructure and connectivity.
Chaya closed by inviting Italian companies to the EU–Tanzania Investment and Business Forum planned for 2027 in Dar es Salaam: “Tanzania is ready to partner, Tanzania is ready to invest, Tanzania is ready to transform.”
After his presentation, Chaya spoke separately with TanzaniaInvest.
He described Italian businesses as positive about Tanzania’s opportunities and said the two countries should build on their long-standing cultural relationship by strengthening trade and investment.
Investors he had met showed particular interest in tax incentives and the energy sector.
“What we have agreed is that we share with them the list of the potential pipeline projects that we have done the feasibility and detailed designs for, so that then they can scrutinize and see which from that list they can be able to finance,” Chaya said, linking stronger trade and investment ties to delivery of Vision 2050.
In a separate conversation with TanzaniaInvest, Andrew Mahiga, Director of Private Investment at the President’s Office for Planning and Investment, highlighted discussions with Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP) on energy financing and Italian interest in rural water and sanitation projects.
He noted that Italian companies had arrived with identified projects and wanted to take discussions further, and that follow-up would benefit from the relevant ministries and decision-makers.
The Tanzanian Ambassador: Italian Company Pursues 50 MW Solar Investment
Tanzania’s Ambassador to Italy, Mbarouk Nassor Mbarouk, told the opening session that he had been informed that morning that an Italian company attending the roadshow was investing in 50 MW of solar power in Tanzania.
He did not identify the company.
Mbarouk also pointed to Italian-Tanzanian cooperation in coffee, including a planned Coffee Training Center in Moshi, and welcomed partnerships in energy storage, efficiency and financing.
Italian Institutions Cite Growing Investment and Business Links
Fabrizio Lobasso, Central Director for the Italian System and Investment at Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, cited USD 8.6 billion in foreign investment registered in Tanzania in the last year, up 56%.
He described the relationship as moving from trade towards productive partnerships in machinery, digitalisation and agricultural logistics.
Patrizia Mauro, Director General of Confindustria Assafrica & Mediterraneo, said Italian interest had accelerated since the launch of the Mattei Plan for Africa.
Members are active in construction, machinery, transport, digital connectivity and training.
Leonardo (Euronext Milan: LDO) and Sparkle were due to present in the afternoon sessions.
Carlo Costa, Vice-President of Cesena Fiera–Macfrut, highlighted mechanisation, irrigation, logistics, cold chains and post-harvest processing.
Carlo Battistini, President of the Chamber of Commerce of Romagna, welcomed the opportunity to connect local firms with Tanzanian partners.
According to Chaya, Italy–Tanzania trade reached about EUR 235 million in 2024.
The 2025 business forum in Dar es Salaam brought together 48 Italian and about 300 Tanzanian companies and generated nearly 500 B2B meetings.
TISEZA: Rice, Cashew, Coffee, Renewable Power and Digital Infrastructure
Gilead J. Teri, Director General of TISEZA, presented opportunities in agriculture, renewable energy and digital infrastructure.
He said TISEZA’s One Stop Facilitation Centre has a dedicated desk for Italian and European investors, assisting with registration, visas and residence permits.
Tanzania produces about 2.2 million tonnes of rice a year.
Teri estimated the rice investment opportunity at USD 200–370 million, spanning irrigation, mechanisation, milling, storage, warehouse-receipt systems, integrated clusters and packaging.
The Government could also hire storage facilities built by investors.
Tanzania produces about 400,000 tonnes of cashew annually, but 90%–95% is processed abroad.
Teri said processing can lift value from USD 1.50 per kilogram to USD 8–12.
Anchor processing plants could require USD 10–50 million, with enabling infrastructure requiring USD 1–15 million.
Coffee opportunities include washing stations, drying, traceability, outgrower platforms, roasting and grinding; Teri noted a 10-year corporate income tax exemption for coffee roasted and processed in Tanzania for export.
In energy, Teri outlined investment routes through government supply, captive power for manufacturers in special economic zones and battery storage to support the grid.

articles.title: United States (U.S.) Broadens African Energy Push as Volz Brings Washington to African Energy Week (AEW) 2026 - Social News XYZ
articles.summary: United States (U.S.) Broadens African Energy Push as Volz Brings Washington to African Energy Week (AEW) 2026  Social News XYZ
articles.full_text:
Download logo
The United States is widening its engagement with Africa’s energy sector, combining government-backed finance, technology partnerships and private-sector investment across markets from Mozambique and Nigeria to Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Josh Volz, Deputy Assistant Secretary for Europe, Eurasia, Africa and the Middle East at the U.S. Department of Energy, will bring that agenda to African Energy Week 2026 in Cape Town from October 12-16.
Volz returns to AEW as Washington’s engagement with African energy markets increasingly spans both hydrocarbons and electricity infrastructure. In April, the U.S. Trade and Development Agency brought energy decision-makers from the DRC, Ethiopia, Kenya and Uganda to the U.S. to meet American companies working on transmission and distribution technologies, including AI-enabled grid systems. The program was designed to connect U.S. technology providers with prospective projects and procurement opportunities in African power markets.
Mozambique illustrates the scale that U.S. financing can bring to an African gas project. In March 2025, the U.S. Export-Import Bank approved a nearly $5 billion loan for TotalEnergies’ Mozambique LNG development, reviving a financing package for the long-delayed project. The original $4.7 billion commitment had been approved during the first Trump administration but required reapproval after construction was suspended in 2021. Meanwhile, ExxonMobil and its Area 4 partners awarded approximately $1.1 billion in pre-investment contracts for long-lead equipment and early construction activities at the Rovuma LNG project in August.
Development finance is another part of the equation. The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation’s investment ceiling rose from $60 billion to $205 billion following its 2025 reauthorization, while the agency gained expanded authority covering international investments in strategic sectors including energy and critical minerals. The new authorization runs through 2031.
The DFC has also continued to approve new transactions in Africa in 2026. On September 16, the agency announced more than $8 billion in new investments globally, including projects supporting infrastructure and resources across Africa, as part of an effort to promote U.S. exports, energy security and American technology.
U.S. companies such as GE Vernova are active across African power markets, providing generation, transmission, grid and software technologies. The company says its technology is installed in more than 50 countries across the Middle East and Africa; in Nigeria alone, its equipment is installed across more than 40 sites, while its grid technology has also supported regional integration through the West African Power Pool.
Energy access is another emerging strand of Washington’s engagement. U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright co-chaired the July 2026 high-level summit on clean cooking in Africa alongside Kenyan President William Ruto, Norway and the International Energy Agency. The meeting produced $900 million in new commitments, taking total commitments since the 2024 Africa Clean Cooking Summit to more than $3.1 billion. Wright described clean cooking as a major but often overlooked energy-access challenge.
Volz has previously argued that African countries should determine their own energy pathways while the United States looks for ways to partner with them. Speaking at AEW 2025, he said: “International governments should not stand in the way of how African nations determine their energy futures. We are eager to hear how best we can, from a U.S. perspective, partner with Africa.” He also pointed to $65 billion in existing U.S. private-sector investment in Africa and a $2.5 billion U.S. government pledge to support energy expansion.
That approach will have a substantial U.S. presence at AEW 2026. The current program confirms Volz alongside U.S. Senator Ted Cruz, United States Energy Association President and CEO Mark W. Menezes and DFC Managing Director and Regional Head of Africa Vibhuti Jain, among other U.S.-linked executives and policymakers. Jain will also participate in the dedicated U.S.-Africa Energy & Investment Forum on October 14, which will bring together U.S. and African companies, investors and policymakers to discuss capital, technology and commercial partnerships.
“The DFC is better resourced than it has ever been, making this an opportune moment for African operators to make their case. This conference is about making sure the capital and the projects actually find each other,” said NJ Ayuk, Executive Chairman of the African Energy Chamber.
For African energy markets, the expanding U.S. role reaches across project finance, LNG, upstream development, electricity infrastructure, grid technology and clean cooking. Volz’s participation at AEW 2026 comes as those relationships increasingly move from broad policy discussions toward individual projects, commercial partnerships and technology deployment across the continent.

In a statement issued by the Special Adviser to the Governor on Media, Dr Sulaimon Olanrewaju, the government said the Botswana maize initiative was initially considered because of its potential to expand cultivation, provide guaranteed off-take for farmers and generate foreign exchange.
The state government, however, said subsequent feasibility studies conducted by the Oyo State Agribusiness Development Agency (OYSADA) indicated that maize production in the state could not meet the scale and price requirements needed for sustainable international export.
According to the statement, “comprehensive feasibility studies conducted by the Oyo State Agribusiness Development Agency revealed that Oyo State did not possess a strong comparative advantage in maize production at the scale and price required for international export.”
The government said the findings informed its decision to redirect attention to agricultural value chains with stronger commercial prospects, particularly cassava production and processing.
Governor Makinde had also publicly explained the change in strategy, saying: “When we took a closer look at the data, it became clear that maize was not the crop we could competitively export at that point. So, we shifted attention to cassava.”
The government said the decision was also influenced by developments in the national maize market, including the Federal Government’s approval of large-scale maize importation, which it said affected local market prices and altered the economics of domestic maize production.
It stated that the administration consequently considered it necessary to avoid exposing Oyo farmers to additional market shocks.
The statement stressed that the decision to abandon the proposed maize export arrangement did not amount to a withdrawal from international agricultural trade.
Rather, it said the administration was pursuing a broader strategy aimed at positioning Oyo State to participate sustainably in regional and continental markets.
The state government pointed to its adoption and implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) strategy as part of efforts to strengthen Oyo’s participation in international trade. In February 2026, the state said it had positioned itself to leverage AfCFTA for export business and industrialisation.
It said the establishment of OYSADA and the development of agribusiness industrial hubs were also central to the administration’s agricultural strategy.

The statement said the administration’s objective was to move agriculture beyond primary production by connecting farmers with processors, investors and markets.

articles.title: African Development Bank and Germany sign pact to boost Africa’s railways - eastleighvoice.co.ke
articles.summary: African Development Bank and Germany sign pact to boost Africa’s railways  eastleighvoice.co.ke
articles.full_text:
The African Development Bank Group has signed a letter of intent with the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) to cooperate on developing Africa's railway systems and deepening regional economic integration.
The agreement was signed during the inaugural African European Industry Dialogue on Railways, held as part of InnoTrans, the International Trade Fair for Transport Technology in Berlin.
Mike Salawou, the Bank Group's Director for Infrastructure and Urban Development, signed on behalf of the institution. Michael Krake, BMZ's Deputy Director General for Economic Cooperation, signed for Germany. The dialogue was jointly organised by the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), Deutsche Bahn, and the EU's Global Gateway initiative.
More To Read
What the partnership will do
Under the agreement, the two entities will work together to reduce Africa's transport costs, improve cross-border interoperability, promote low-carbon transport solutions, embed sustainable transport policies, and build a robust local labour market in the railway sector through skills transfer and vocational training.
Cooperation will begin with a joint feasibility study for an African Rail Competence Centre, to be implemented by GIZ and expected to launch by October 2026. The Centre would bring together innovation and training to modernise and expand Africa's railways.
The scale of the challenge
Africa's rail network represents only 8 to 10 per cent of the world's total. The continent has roughly 90,000 kilometres of railway lines, but much of it is fragmented, ageing, or designed for extraction rather than integration. Colonial-era lines were built to move minerals and agricultural goods from hinterlands to ports—not to connect African countries.
Different gauges, poor maintenance, and missing links mean that a train from Mombasa cannot easily reach Kigali, and a wagon from Lobito cannot roll seamlessly into Lusaka.
The African Continental Free Trade Area, which creates a market of over 1.4 billion people, is driving growing demand for cross-border freight and passenger movement. But without functional railways, that demand will be met by trucks on roads that are often congested, costly, and unsafe. Road transport accounts for 80 to 90 per cent of freight movement in Africa, compared with 20 to 30 per cent in Europe and the United States.
The bank's portfolio
In his keynote address, Salawou pointed to the Bank's existing investments in the Lobito Corridor, the Standard Gauge Railway programme in East Africa, the Nacala Corridor, Algeria's North-South Rail Corridor, Morocco's high-speed rail system, and urban rail projects in Senegal and Nigeria.
The Lobito Corridor—a 1,300-kilometre railway linking Angola's Atlantic coast to the mineral belts of the DRC and Zambia—has become a flagship for Western infrastructure engagement in Africa. The United States and the European Union have both backed the project, seeing it as a counterweight to Chinese infrastructure dominance on the continent.
The Standard Gauge Railway in Kenya, meanwhile, has been a model and a cautionary tale. It transformed connectivity between Mombasa and Nairobi, but its cost, debt burden, and limited extension have raised questions about sustainability.
The five priorities
Salawou set out five priorities for the sector: a continental market driven by AfCFTA, modal-shift reforms, interoperable standards, financing that crowds in private capital, and the competencies needed to operate the networks once built.
"Building a railway is half the job," he said. "Running it is the harder half."
That line captures the essence of the challenge. Africa has no shortage of railway ambitions. It has a shortage of functioning railways. The difference lies not in construction but in maintenance, operations, regulation, and skills.
What Germany brings
Krake emphasised BMZ's long-standing commitment to supporting Africa's development. "BMZ is committed to working with our African partners to strengthen regional connectivity and support sustainable economic development," he said. "Together with the African Development Bank, we will advance practical cooperation on interoperability, skills development and other priorities that help build a stronger railway sector."
Germany brings technical expertise, vocational training models, and financing. The EU's Global Gateway initiative—Europe's answer to China's Belt and Road—provides the broader strategic framework.

articles.title: Poland’s Journey towards High-Speed Rail - railwaypro.com
articles.summary: Poland’s Journey towards High-Speed Rail  railwaypro.com
articles.full_text:
The Port Polska railway programme is crucial to Poland’s development. On the new High-Speed Rail lines, trains will be able to reach speeds of up to 320–350 km/h. This represents a major technological leap, but Polish railway professionals have understood since the very beginning of the railway era that speed and journey time are among the factors that matter most to passengers.
The history of increasing speeds on Poland’s railways is a process that has lasted for more than a century – from the first steam locomotives exceeding 100 km/h, through the period of the Polish People’s Republic and record-breaking runs on the Central Rail Line (Centralna Magistrala Kolejowa – CMK), to the era of Pendolino trains and preparations for the construction of a High-Speed Rail network.
- 1936 – The era of the “Luxtorpeda”: The famous diesel railcar set an unofficial record on the Kraków–Zakopane route, completing the journey in 2 hours and 18 minutes – a record that remains unbeaten to this day. The Luxtorpeda had a design speed of 115 km/h.
- 1937 – The Pm36 steam locomotive: The Polish Pm36-1 express steam locomotive, fitted with an aerodynamic casing, won a gold medal at the Exposition Internationale des Arts et Techniques in Paris. It could reach speeds of up to 140 km/h.
- 1977 – Opening of the CMK: The Central Rail Line (Zawiercie–Grodzisk Mazowiecki) was opened. By the 1980s, trains on the CMK were already operating at speeds of up to 140 km/h. The line was designed from the outset for speeds of 200–250 km/h, which was exceptional for the Eastern Bloc at the
- 1994 – The first Pendolino record: During testing on the CMK, the Italian ETR460 Pendolino set a Central and Eastern European speed record, reaching 250.1 km/h.
- 2013 – Poland’s absolute railway speed record: During testing on the CMK, the new ED250 trainset – the Pendolino trains purchased by PKP Intercity – reached 293 km/h. This remains the official speed record on Polish railway tracks.
- 2014 – Regular operation at 200 km/h: In December 2014, Express InterCity Premium (Pendolino) trains began regular passenger services at speeds of 200 km/h on selected sections of the
This is, of course, not the end of the story. Poland, as a modern country, is taking on increasingly advanced technologies and challenges. This is why, as part of the Port Polska programme, we are building railway infrastructure that will allow trains to operate at speeds of up to 350 km/h.
The new HSR lines will provide an entirely new quality of travel across the country, not only on routes such as Warsaw–Wrocław or Warsaw–Poznań, but also on other connections, including Białystok, Jelenia Góra, Lublin and Szczecin, using the high-speed network. Completely new infrastructure must deliver a very clear reduction in journey times compared with existing lines.
New lines, new rolling stock
At present, infrastructure development is being planned to parameters resulting from European regulations, namely up to 350 km/h. The rolling stock being ordered is also expected to meet these requirements, as it should remain in service on the network potentially until as late as 2070.
“We cannot be afraid of these parameters if they give us a clear reduction in journey times between the main centres. Completely new railway infrastructure must deliver a clear difference in journey times compared with existing lines,” says Piotr Malepszak, Deputy Minister of Infrastructure.
He added that reaching the target speed on the railway will be preceded by intermediate steps. One such step will be the introduction of 250 km/h operation on the CMK as early as next year.
“Then, after 2030, speeds will begin to increase to more than 300 km/h. We are already operating at 200 km/h and we are continuing to gain experience with this speed,” the Deputy Minister said.
Port Polska – transforming Poland’s railway
The Port Polska programme goes beyond the construction of individual high-speed railway lines. At its centre is the planned “Y” high-speed railway line, which will connect Warsaw, the new national airport, Łódź and, via a fork at Sieradz, Poznań and Wrocław.
The line is approximately 480 km long and is being developed for speeds of up to 350 km/h. Its technical parameters – including track geometry, gradients, curve radii, overhead line equipment and turnouts – are designed to support high-speed operation. The first section, connecting Warsaw, the new airport and Łódź, is planned to open by the end of 2032.
According to Port Polska, the “Y” is intended to form the backbone of Poland’s new high-speed railway system. The project is being developed not only to increase maximum speeds, but above all to achieve substantial reductions in journey times between the country’s largest urban centres. The infrastructure is being designed for an operating speed of up to 350 km/h, with the fastest services expected to be scheduled at around 320 km/h, while operation at up to 350 km/h will be possible for suitable rolling stock.
The “Y” is also part of a much broader vision for Poland’s railway network. In June 2026, Port Polska presented the Integrated Railway Network (Zintegrowana Sieć Kolejowa – ZSK), described as the first comprehensive long-term plan for the development of Poland’s railway network.
The ZSK envisages around 4,700 km of new railway lines, of which approximately 1,000 km are already under construction, in procurement or at an advanced design stage. The plan includes 19 major railway corridors and would provide 27 small and medium-sized towns with access to the railway network. Around 2,700 km of the planned new lines would be built to High-Speed Rail standards, including the 480-km “Y” line.
The wider plan also includes the extension of the Central Rail Line towards northern Poland, as well as new connections in different regions of the country. In total, the programme envisages the modernisation of approximately 5,600 km of existing railway lines after 2035.
The objective is therefore not simply to build faster railway lines, but to create a more integrated national network, connecting Poland’s major cities and regions while improving access to rail for smaller centres. According to Port Polska, the ZSK is intended to support the long-term development of passenger and freight rail and provide the basis for railway investment over the coming decades.
The “Y” and the ZSK therefore represent the next stage in Poland’s long history of increasing railway speeds – moving from isolated high-speed achievements towards a nationwide railway system designed around shorter journey times, higher speeds and improved connectivity

articles.title: Fixing Nigeria’s eroding sovereignty - vanguardngr.com
articles.summary: Fixing Nigeria’s eroding sovereignty  vanguardngr.com
articles.full_text:
Sixty-six years after independence, Nigeria’s sovereignty is formally intact, but its practical authority over territory and security has been weakened by persistent violence and the inability to guarantee safety in every community. The country that once appeared destined to become Africa’s giant now marks another Independence Day amid insecurity, economic strain and massive distrust. The long descent began in the First Republic. Political rivalry, regional suspicion and constitutional weaknesses culminated in the January 1966 coup, which killed Prime Minister Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, Ahmadu Bello, Samuel Akintola and other leaders. The July counter-coup, pogroms against easterners and collapse of trust eventually produced Biafra’s secession in 1967 and the civil war, which ended in 1970. Thereafter came prolonged military rule, coups, political instability and economic decline.
Nigeria has repeatedly failed to turn diversity into strength. More than 387 ethnic groups and over 500 languages should constitute a reservoir of culture, enterprise and creativity. Instead, political entrepreneurs have too often weaponised identity, religion and grievance for electoral advantage, making citizenship increasingly subordinate to primordial loyalties. The consequences include mutual suspicion, separatist agitations, jihadist insurgencies and violent crimes. Today, sovereignty is tested by armed groups. Boko Haram and Islamic State-linked insurgents continue operating in the North-East, while banditry and kidnapping have spread across the North-West, North-Central and beyond. Armed Fulani herdsmen have been attacking and displacing communities, especially in the Middle Belt areas, with threats in every state of the federation. Recent mass abductions, including nearly 700 people reportedly taken in Niger State in August 2026, underline the continuing challenge.
Our gallant security forces have achieved important successes, including joint Nigeria–US counterterrorism operations, but the persistence and geographical spread of armed violence show that force alone has not restored security. This is where sovereignty becomes uncomfortable. America’s limited military intervention, which was couched as “cooperation”, said it loud and clear that we need help to fix our compromised sovereignty.
Despite our sorry situation, Nigeria still matters enormously. It is Africa’s most populous country. It possesses major energy resources, has a globally influential film and music industry, and produces leaders of international stature. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala remains Director-General of the World Trade Organisation, while Nigeria continues to command diplomatic, commercial and cultural attention. The difficult road back requires effective constitutionalism, accountable federalism and genuine inclusion. Nepotism must give way to competence and representation. Federal appointments should respect constitutional principles and reassure every community that Nigeria belongs to all. Security forces need intelligence, technology and mobility, while justice must accompany force. Armed insurgency of all types must be defeated.
The 2027 elections should be a civic opportunity for Nigerians to elect leaders committed to constitutional government, security, economic productivity and inclusion. Beyond elections, Nigeria must invest in education, jobs, infrastructure, justice and independent and accountable institutions. Independence is not merely the absence of colonial rule. It is the capacity of a nation to secure its people, govern itself fairly and convert diversity into shared prosperity.
Nigeria can still reclaim her dream. It is a task that must be done!

articles.title: Africa must turn MICE into a $1.3tn deal-making engine – Lai Mohammed - Nigerian NewsDirect

Former Minister of Information and Culture, Alhaji Lai Mohammed, has urged African governments to transform MICE into a major deal-making engine.
Mohammed made the call at the ninth Africa Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions (MICE) Summit in Mombasa, Kenya, where he advocated using business events to drive investment, trade and employment.
A text of presentation of the former minister was made available to newsmen on Saturday in Abuja.
Mohammed said the global MICE industry was worth about 1.3 trillion dollars, while Africa accounted for only four per cent.
“MICE should not be seen simply as people coming to Africa, staying in hotels, eating in restaurants and flying home,” he said.
Mohammed said MICE could bring investors, buyers, policymakers, experts and businesses into African economies, thereby creating opportunities for investment, partnerships and job creation.
He urged African destinations to develop MICE strategies around their comparative advantages instead of competing blindly for the same international events.
He cited Nigeria’s entertainment industry, Kenya’s athletics and tourism, South Africa’s conference industry and Rwanda’s business gateway as examples of distinctive African strengths.
Mohammed also advocated greater cooperation among African countries, including joint bids for major international events and shared hosting arrangements.
He cited the 2026 FIFA World Cup, jointly hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, as a model Africa could consider.
Using Lagos as a case study, Mohammed said the city’s cultural and economic assets could be developed into major MICE opportunities.
He recalled a study commissioned while he was minister which indicated that about 20,000 events were held in Lagos every month.
Mohammed said the growth of “Detty December” demonstrated how events could create interconnected opportunities across aviation, hospitality, transport, entertainment, media, fashion, technology and retail.
“The opportunity is to turn events into ecosystems,” he said.
The former minister, who chairs the Eko Tourism Foundation, identified infrastructure, intra-African connectivity and visa restrictions as major barriers to MICE development.
He said hotels, convention centres, airports, transport systems, digital infrastructure and reliable utilities were essential for attracting major international events.
Mohammed called for improved air connectivity, e-visas, visa-on-arrival arrangements where appropriate and fast-track processing for accredited conference delegates.
He said MICE development could not be separated from the wider investment environment, warning that uncertainty and weak institutions could undermine investor confidence.
“Africa does not only have to sell its opportunities. It has to sell credibility,” he said.
Mohammed said smaller countries could become significant MICE destinations by positioning themselves as platforms, citing Rwanda as an example.
He urged governments to change how they measure the success of business events, beyond delegate numbers and hotel occupancy.
He said authorities should measure investments attracted, business meetings held, trade generated, partnerships created and jobs resulting from such events.
Mohammed also called for every African country to establish an empowered National Convention Bureau to coordinate MICE development and economic impact measurement.
He said such agencies should bid for major events, coordinate public-private efforts, facilitate business visitors and gather MICE intelligence.
“The true measure of a successful business event is not simply how many people attended, but what happened because they attended,” he said.
He asked whether investments came, trade relationships began, business partnerships emerged or jobs were created after events.
“That is when MICE stops being merely an event, and becomes an engine of economic transformation,” Mohammed said.
Delegates from 19 countries attended the two-day summit, formally opened by Mohamed Osman Ali, Mombasa County Executive for Tourism, Culture and Trade.

From Aidoghie Paulinus, Abuja
Former Minister of Information and Culture, Alhaji Lai Mohammed, has given reasons why African governments must reposition Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions (MICE) as an instrument for driving trade, investment, business partnerships and job creation, rather than treating it primarily as a tourism activity.
The former minister spoke at the just-concluded ninth edition of the Africa MICE Summit in Mombasa, Kenya, with the theme: ‘Building Africa’s MICE Economies.’
The global MICE industry is estimated at about US$1.3 trillion, yet Africa accounts for only about four percent of the enormous market, underscoring the vast opportunity available to the continent.
Delegates from 19 countries attended the two-day event, which was formally opened by the County Executive Council Member, Tourism, Culture and Trade, County of Mombasa, Mohamed Osman Ali.
Mohammed said MICE could become a major economic engine for Africa by bringing investors, buyers, policymakers, experts and businesses together.
“MICE should not be seen simply as people coming to Africa, staying in hotels, eating in restaurants and flying home. MICE is an economic instrument. It can bring investors, buyers, policymakers, experts and businesses into our economies. In other words, MICE can become Africa’s deal-making engine,” Mohammed said.
Mohammed who was a panellist at the event, urged African destinations to build their MICE strategies around their comparative advantages, rather than competing blindly for the same events.
He cited Nigeria’s globally-acclaimed entertainment industry, Kenya’s strength in athletics and tourism, South Africa’s conference industry and Rwanda’s position as a regional business gateway and advocated greater cooperation among African countries, including joint bids for major international events.
While proposing that Africa bid collectively for major global events and share hosting among countries, as Canada, Mexico and the United States did for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Mohammed referenced Lagos as a case study of how local cultural and economic assets can be transformed into major MICE opportunities.
He recalled a study commissioned while he was minister which indicated that about 20,000 events were held in Lagos every month, and pointed to the growth of “Detty December” as an example of an event ecosystem involving aviation, hospitality, transportation, entertainment, media, fashion, technology and retail.
“The opportunity is to turn events into ecosystems,” the former minister also said.
Mohammed who chairs the Board of Trustees and the Governing Council of the Eko Tourism Foundation (ETF), however, identified infrastructure, intra-African connectivity and visa restrictions as major obstacles to the growth of the sector.
According to the former minister, hotels, convention centres, airports, transport systems, digital infrastructure and reliable utilities are essential to attracting major international events.
He further called for easier movement across Africa through improved air connectivity, e-visas, visa-on-arrival arrangements where appropriate and fast-track processing for accredited conference delegates.
Noting that MICE cannot be separated from the wider investment environment, Mohammed warned that political uncertainty, policy reversals, weak institutions and corruption undermined investor confidence.
“Africa does not only have to sell its opportunities. It has to sell credibility,” he added.
Mohammed also argued that smaller countries can become significant MICE destinations by positioning themselves as platforms rather than simply markets, citing Rwanda as an example.
On the policy shift required, he said African governments must change the way they measure the success of business events.
“Instead of asking only how many delegates attended or how many hotel nights were generated, they should ask: How many investors attended? How many business meetings took place? How much investment and trade were generated? How many jobs were created?” Mohammed stated.
He called on every African country to establish an empowered National Convention Bureau responsible for bidding for major events, coordinating public and private-sector efforts, facilitating business visitors, gathering MICE intelligence and measuring economic impact.
Mohammed said the true measure of a successful business event was not simply how many people attended, but what happened because they attended.
“Did an investment come? Did a trade relationship begin? Did a business partnership emerge? Did jobs get created?
“That is when MICE stops being merely an event, and becomes an engine of economic transformation,” he concluded.

articles.title: Stability not luxury, essential for economic development: El-Sisi at Alamein-Africa Forum - Foreign Affairs - Egypt - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Stability not luxury, essential for economic development: El-Sisi at Alamein-Africa Forum - Foreign Affairs - Egypt  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi stressed on Saturday that economic development cannot be built in unstable countries, and that stability is not a luxury but a fundamental pillar sought by investors, manufacturers and farmers to operate in a safe environment that enables them to achieve their objectives.
El-Sisi’s remarks came during the inaugural Alamein-Africa Business Forum, taking place in New Alamein City from 2 to 4 October.
During his speech, the president said the forum is taking place at a critical juncture, as the world is experiencing successive crises and rapid transformations, with geopolitical tensions intertwined with economic and development challenges, while global production, energy and technology landscapes are being reshaped.
He stressed that, amidst these circumstances, countries must strengthen their capabilities to enhance resilience and build their own future and that of their peoples.
In Africa, security begins with supporting national states and their institutions, respecting their unity and sovereignty, prioritizing peaceful solutions to conflicts and crises, and upholding good-neighbourliness principles, El-Sisi said.
These principles, he added, would help advance cooperation and economic integration to fulfil African peoples’ aspirations for development and prosperity.
El-Sisi reaffirmed Egypt’s steadfast commitment to supporting this vision, citing the country’s pride in its deep-rooted African identity and its efforts to launch and support development and economic initiatives across the continent.
He affirmed Cairo’s firm belief that Africa’s renaissance, independence and the prosperity of its peoples are legitimate rights that must be upheld and preserved.
During his speech, El-Sisi said the forum, approved under an African Union (AU) decision at its February 2026 summit, reflects the interconnection between political and economic endeavors within the framework of joint African action.
It also provides a strategic continental platform to mobilize efforts towards achieving the AU’s Agenda 2063 and translating the aspirations of joint African action into tangible results, the president added.
The forum, El-Sisi said, also offers a unique platform for African businesses to engage with national leaders, discuss challenges facing the private sector and establish cross-border partnerships to advance economic integration, and achieve continental development goals
Citing statistics on the continent’s economic landscape, El-Sisi said the African private sector stands as the most significant driver of the continent's economies, contributing more than 70 percent of the continent’s gross domestic product (GDP).
However, the president added, around 85 percent of its transactions are conducted with companies outside Africa, while more than half of small and medium-sized enterprises lack sufficient information about available opportunities in neighbouring African markets, prompting them to seek commercial opportunities in distant international markets.
Despite existing trade agreements and preferential arrangements linking the continent's nations, intra-African trade has accounted for only around 18 percent of the continent’s total trade in recent years, he said.
El-Sisi said that against this backdrop, the forum’s idea has emerged, as an institutional bridge to overcome isolation and close information gaps by facilitating direct communication between private-sector representatives and investors across Africa.
The event would also help building effective platforms for closer ties and empowering the African private sector to explore its untapped opportunities, contribute to implementing the African Continental Free Trade Area agreement (AfCFTA) and advance the continent’s development goals under Agenda 2063.
During his speech, El-Sisi described Africa as a young and vibrant continent, as young people account for around 65 percent of its population, and highlighted its vast natural and human resources.
He said African countries were increasingly engaging with growing influence in the international community and seeking to become key partners in shaping the global order.
Africa, he added, looks forward to a world characterized by peace and stability, rather than one in which African countries bear the repercussions and grapple with the negative consequences of global crises in which they played no part.
The current global energy crisis illustrates these challenges, he said, pointing to rising fuel and fertilizer prices, disruptions to supply and shipping chains, and other repercussions that are placing additional pressure on African economies.
“Our objective is clear: to build modern states capable of keeping pace with rapid global economic transformations and shaping a fairer and more sustainable future. Let us move forward together to achieve this goal,” El-Sisi said.
He expressed confidence that the 21st century could be an African century par excellence, if the continent strengthened its joint efforts.
El-Sisi called on forum participants to engage actively in its various tracks to identify genuine opportunities and new horizons for cooperation.
“We hope that the panel discussions will witness an effective exchange of insights and solutions, and that the bilateral business meetings, along with the opportunities offered by the exhibition, will succeed in fostering further cross-border commercial partnerships,” he said.
The president highlighted the need to give special attention to the startups platform, which represents a promising future for our African economies.
During his speech, El-Sisi welcomed participants to New Alamein City, describing it as a place that had witnessed major historical events, including one of the largest battles of World War II, and had since become a model of development and prosperity.
The forum’s opening session featured remarks by the Minister of Foreign Affairs Badr Abdelatty, President of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) George Elombi, Director-General of the African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD) Nardos Bekele-Thomas, Chairperson of the African Union (AU) Commission Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, President of the Dangote Group Aliko Dangote, and Burundian President and Chairperson of the AU Évariste Ndayishimiye.
Following the conclusion of the forum’s opening session, President El-Sisi and African heads of state and delegation leaders toured the economic exhibition held on the sidelines of the forum.
During the tour, they were briefed on the key programs and projects being implemented by the exhibitors to achieve continental integration.
They also visited the pavilions of Egypt, Afreximbank, and AUDA-NEPAD.
According to the Egyptian presidency, the first edition of the forum includes a number of specialized sessions addressing key economic and development issues of priority to the African continent.
It also features an exhibition for major African companies, as well as a dedicated area for start-ups, with broad participation by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) from various African countries.
The forum’s activities also include numerous bilateral and multilateral meetings among government officials, corporate leaders, and representatives of financial and economic institutions, thereby bolstering opportunities for cooperation, investment, and cross-border partnerships.
Organized by the Egyptian government, the AU Commission, AUDA-NEPAD, and Afreximbank, the Alamein-Africa forum, an outcome of an Egyptian initiative endorsed by the AU, is set to be held every two years in New Alamein City.
The inaugural edition of the forum is being held with high-level participation, including a number of African heads of state and senior continental officials, as well as leading figures from international and regional business and financial institutions and private-sector leaders from Africa and across the globe.
The forum serves as a strategic platform for strengthening communication and partnerships among African governments, private-sector representatives, and entrepreneurs from within and outside the continent.
This contributes to maximizing the role of the private sector in advancing comprehensive and sustainable development efforts in Africa and accelerating the implementation of the objectives of the AU’s Agenda 2063.
The forum also aims to stimulate intra-African trade, foster economic integration among the African countries, mobilize the partnerships required to implement development projects, expand financing and investment opportunities, and support promising and emerging economic sectors.

Damerjog-Dewele Pipeline Project Reflects Ethiopia’s Era of Renewal: Scholars
Addis Ababa, October 3, 2026 (ENA)— The Damerjog-Dewele Petroleum Products Pipeline Project will accelerate Ethiopia’s economic growth, strengthen fuel security and deepen economic ties between Ethiopia and Djibouti, scholars said.
The 120-kilometer petroleum products pipeline, which will connect Damerjog in Djibouti with Dewele in Ethiopia, is among the major infrastructure projects being undertaken to support Ethiopia’s economic transformation and improve the efficiency of fuel supply.
The construction of the project was recently launched by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Djiboutian President Ismail Omar Guelleh and Dangote Group President Aliko Dangote.
The project is being implemented through a partnership between Ethiopian Investment Holdings and the Dangote Group.
During the launching ceremony, it was stated that the pipeline will have the capacity to store and transport more than one million cubic meters of refined petroleum products.
Professor Tassew Woldehanna, President of the Ethiopian Economics Association and a lecturer in the Department of Economics at Addis Ababa University, told ENA that the newly launched Ethiopia-Djibouti petroleum pipeline demonstrates Ethiopia’s growing commitment to strategic investment and economic infrastructure.
He said Ethiopia’s longstanding reliance on road transport to import petroleum products from Djibouti has posed challenges to maintaining a reliable and efficient national fuel supply.
The Damerjog-Dewele pipeline is therefore expected to help address these challenges by providing a dedicated infrastructure system for transporting petroleum products into Ethiopia, he said.
Professor Tassew also emphasized that the significance of an investment should be assessed not only by its contribution to economic growth but also by the employment and business opportunities it creates.
In this regard, he said, the pipeline project could generate economic opportunities while supporting activities across various sectors.
Economist Birhanu Alemu, for his part, said Ethiopia’s expanding infrastructure development and economic activities require the country to strengthen its petroleum storage and distribution capacity.
Given the growing scale of commercial and productive activities, increasing national fuel reserves is essential to ensuring the continuity of economic operations, he said.
From this perspective, the Damerjog-Dewele pipeline will play an important role in ensuring a more reliable and stable fuel supply and reducing disruptions associated with conventional fuel transportation, Birhanu noted.
He further explained that a dependable petroleum supply is critical to manufacturing industries, mechanized agriculture and the transport sector, all of which are essential to increasing productivity and supporting economic growth.
The scholars said major infrastructure projects being initiated and implemented by Ethiopia could contribute not only to the country’s economic transformation but also to broader regional development.
They cited the Damerjog-Dewele pipeline as an example of how infrastructure cooperation between neighboring countries can create shared economic benefits.
The project is also expected to strengthen economic interdependence between Ethiopia and Djibouti by improving the movement of strategic commodities and expanding opportunities for investment and trade.
According to the scholars, such joint infrastructure initiatives can further consolidate the longstanding relations between the two countries while contributing to regional economic integration.
Overall, they said the Damerjog-Dewele Petroleum Products Pipeline reflects Ethiopia’s broader development drive under its national vision of transforming infrastructure, strengthening productive capacity and creating the foundations for sustained economic growth.
