articles.full_text:
Tanzanian Firms Invest Just 11% of What They Did a Decade Ago
Ready
The average Tanzanian firm now invests only 11% of what it did a decade ago, according to the World Bank. Weak long term finance, technology adoption, innovation and land access are limiting the private sector’s ability to raise productivity and create better jobs.
Tanzania’s economy is growing above 6%, private sector credit is expanding rapidly and major public infrastructure projects continue to raise economy wide investment. Yet inside the ordinary Tanzanian firm, investment has moved sharply in the opposite direction. The World Bank’s new Tanzania Economic Update: Making Jobs Work finds that the average firm now invests only 11% of what it did a decade ago. The share of firms purchasing fixed assets fell from 40% in 2013 to 22% in 2023, while average investment declined from about $116,000 to $24,000 in constant 2009 dollars. The fall cuts across firm sizes and sectors and is particularly pronounced among medium sized businesses and manufacturers.
The finding deserves more attention than the headline GDP number because firm investment is one of the main mechanisms through which growth becomes productivity. Businesses raise output per worker when they buy better machinery, expand factories, adopt software, improve production processes, develop new products and enter larger markets. When firms stop investing, the economy can continue growing for a period through government spending, construction, population growth or higher commodity prices, but the productive capacity of the private sector changes more slowly. Tanzania’s recent growth therefore contains a difficult contrast: national investment remains visible, yet the average private firm appears to be upgrading less.
The World Bank’s latest Tanzania Economic Update places this decline inside a larger jobs problem. Tanzania does not primarily lack people who are working. Nearly 69% of working age Tanzanians are employed. What it lacks is a sufficiently large base of firms productive enough to pay higher wages and employ more workers in formal, stable jobs. The Bank’s diagnosis is unusually direct: labour productivity among Tanzanian formal firms is around 49% below Sub Saharan African peers in services and approximately 70% lower in manufacturing.
Why Are Tanzanian Firms Investing Less?
The World Bank links weak firm investment to several constraints that reinforce one another. Long term finance remains scarce, business expansion can be complicated by land access and regulatory requirements, technology adoption is weak and many firms operate at productivity levels too low to generate enough retained earnings for major reinvestment. One in three Tanzanian firms reports being fully or partly credit constrained, compared with about 22% across Sub Saharan African comparators. Only 14% of Tanzanian firms finance investment through banks, compared with 25% in Rwanda and 38% in Côte d’Ivoire, while bank finance covers only about 4% of investment expenditure among Tanzanian firms that use it.
Those figures reveal a financing problem that is more specific than saying businesses lack credit. Tanzanian banks are lending. Private sector credit was growing at 28.1% year on year by June 2026, a multi year high. The weakness is the type and maturity of financing available to firms. Commercial banks remain oriented towards short term lending, including trade finance and working capital, while machinery, factories, new production lines and technology often require financing over several years. The corporate bond market remains shallow, relatively few companies are listed on the Dar es Salaam Stock Exchange and development finance institutions do not yet provide enough long term capital to fill the gap.
Credit growth can therefore be strong while productive investment remains weak. A loan financing inventory for several months and a loan financing industrial machinery for ten years both appear as private credit, but they have very different effects on productive capacity. Tanzania’s 28% credit growth becomes considerably more important when examined through this distinction.
Why Does Falling Firm Investment Matter for Productivity?
Investment determines how much value a worker can produce with each hour of labour. A worker operating old equipment, relying on manual processes and selling an unchanged product into a small market can work hard without generating high output. Give the same worker better machinery, reliable technology, stronger management systems and access to larger markets and the value of the worker’s output can rise substantially without the number of hours worked changing.
This helps explain why the World Bank places firm productivity at the centre of Tanzania’s jobs challenge. Formal firms with at least five workers produce substantially less output per employee than comparable firms elsewhere in Sub Saharan Africa. Within Tanzania itself, the productivity differences are even larger. The most productive 10% of firms are about 32 times more productive than the least productive 10%. Among retailers, the gap reaches 42 times, while the most productive food processors generate roughly 18 times the sales per worker of the least productive.
A fall in investment makes those gaps harder to close. Businesses at the bottom of the productivity distribution need capital to improve equipment, technology, logistics and production methods. If they cannot finance those upgrades, weaker firms remain weak while a small group of highly productive businesses continues to dominate output. Tanzania then ends up with pockets of excellent firms without a sufficiently large productive middle capable of employing workers at scale.
Are Tanzanian Firms Adopting Enough Technology?
The investment problem extends into technology and innovation. According to the World Bank report, only about 4% of Tanzanian manufacturing firms license technology from foreign companies, compared with 11% among Sub Saharan African peers. Around 7% of Tanzanian firms spend on research and development compared with 13% regionally, while 34% have a website compared with 42% among peer economies.
The product and process numbers are equally weak. Only 9.5% of surveyed Tanzanian firms reported introducing a new production process during the previous three years, against 14.8% among Sub Saharan African firms. Just 14.1% introduced a new product or service compared with 24.6% among regional peers.
These are not merely technology statistics. They describe the speed at which businesses renew themselves. Firms increase productivity when they find ways to produce the same output with fewer inputs, produce better goods at the same cost or enter markets where customers will pay more for what they produce. Machinery, software, research and new production methods are the channels through which those changes occur.
An economy where firms invest less and innovate less can still expand, particularly when government spending, construction and population growth are strong. It will have a harder time increasing income per worker.
Is Tanzania Investing More as an Economy While Firms Invest Less?
One of the most revealing observations in the World Bank report is that falling firm level investment is occurring alongside rising investment in the national accounts. The Bank says the difference probably reflects the strong contribution of construction and large public infrastructure projects to economy wide investment.
This separates two very different investment stories. Tanzania has invested heavily in roads, railways, electricity, ports and other large projects that can increase the productive potential of the economy. Those investments are important because private firms need transport, electricity and communications infrastructure to operate efficiently. But infrastructure does not automatically produce firm level upgrading.
A railway can reduce freight costs, but a manufacturer still needs capital to buy machinery. A stronger electricity grid can improve reliability, but a food processor still needs financing to expand production. A new road can open a market, but a small business still needs working capital and technology to serve that market competitively.
Public infrastructure and private capital formation therefore have to complement one another. Tanzania risks underusing expensive infrastructure if the firms expected to exploit it remain too small, too weakly financed or too technologically limited to expand production.
The policy question should increasingly move from how much Tanzania is investing to where the investment is occurring and whether it is producing enough productive private capacity.
Why Does Long Term Finance Remain Difficult?
The World Bank describes long term investment finance as scarce and expensive. The banking system is still structurally better suited to shorter term commercial lending than to financing assets whose returns may take several years to materialise. Only 14% of firms use banks to finance investment, and even then bank funding represents a very small share of the investment being made.
This is especially restrictive for manufacturing. Buying industrial machinery, building a plant or adding another production line requires large upfront expenditure followed by a long period over which the investment generates returns. Financing that asset with short maturity credit creates a mismatch between when the borrower must repay and when the investment produces enough cash.
Rwanda provides a useful regional comparison in the World Bank data. A quarter of Rwandan firms finance investment through banks, compared with 14% in Tanzania, while banks fund about 16% of the investment undertaken by those firms compared with only 4% in Tanzania. Côte d’Ivoire performs even better on the first measure, with 38% of firms using bank financing for investment.

- Rheinmetall Denel Munition plans to start a LongClaw production line in the second half of 2027.
- The company says the South African designed glide bomb has a range of about 15 km when released from roughly 4.9 km.
- It is aimed mainly at military drones, although the company says it can also be launched from crewed aircraft.
- Small quantities are being assembled manually; no South African military order or export contract was announced.
Rheinmetall Denel Munition, known as RDM, expects to start a production line for its LongClaw glide bomb in the second half of 2027, according to its chief executive, Maximilian Froch.
The weapon weighs 7.5 kilograms and carries a 3-kilogram warhead. RDM says it can travel about 15 kilometres when released from an altitude of roughly 4.9 kilometres. That range describes a particular release condition- it is not a fixed distance the bomb would travel from every altitude.

LongClaw is designed chiefly for unmanned aircraft. Unlike a drone that flies into its target, it is a separate weapon released by an aircraft. Its wings allow it to glide towards a target, while a satellite-based system guides it.
RDM says small quantities are already being assembled manually and that the weapon has undergone evaluation on several drone platforms. The company has not announced that a full production line is operating, nor has it identified a confirmed buyer.
He said LongClaw was designed entirely in South Africa and that most of its components would be made locally. “We have tried to have the most indigenous solution possible,” he said.
A South African design in a German group’s portfolio
RDM is a South African company jointly owned by Rheinmetall’s German ammunition business, which holds 51%, and South African state defence company Denel, which holds the remainder.

It already produces other types of ammunition and markets products internationally. Rheinmetall identified LongClaw as a drone-deployable glide bomb when presenting its defence products in June.
That makes the production plan significant for South Africa’s defence industry. A locally designed weapon could be manufactured through a company with established international sales channels, though that does not guarantee export orders.
RDM says it is also trying to interest the South African National Defence Force in LongClaw. Froch told DefenceWeb that international sales would require approval from South Africa’s arms export authorities. Neither domestic procurement nor an overseas sale was announced.
Mock-ups of the bomb were displayed on two South African aircraft designs at September’s Africa Aerospace and Defence exhibition, Paramount’s V-Raven drone and its Mwari aircraft. A display showing how a weapon could be carried should not be mistaken for confirmation that either aircraft has entered service with LongClaw.
For now, LongClaw’s confirmed position is narrower than a completed military upgrade: it is a South African designed weapon undergoing development and evaluation, with a production line planned for next year.

articles.title: Alamein-Africa Forum seeks to turn continent’s potential into investment: Egypt PM - Foreign Affairs - Egypt - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Alamein-Africa Forum seeks to turn continent’s potential into investment: Egypt PM - Foreign Affairs - Egypt  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said on Friday that the inaugural Alamein-Africa Forum aims to turn the continent’s economic potential into investment and concrete projects by bringing governments, businesses, and development and financial institutions together on a permanent biennial platform.
The Egyptian PM made the remarks during the welcome session of the inaugural Alamein-Africa Forum, held from 2 to 4 October in New Alamein City.
Madbouly said the forum is intended to provide a sustainable space for dialogue among governments, the private sector, and financing and development institutions, and will be held every two years in Egypt.
The forum is being held in line with African Union decisions aimed at strengthening the private sector’s role in development and economic integration across the continent. The AU Summit approved holding the forum biennially in New Alamein in February 2026.
Madbouly said the inaugural edition represents the beginning of a process that Egypt hopes will expand from one edition to the next, allowing partnerships, expertise, and projects to accumulate.
Madbouly said choosing New Alamein to host the inaugural edition carries a message of its own, describing the city as an example of what ambitious plans can achieve when combined with infrastructure investment and implementation.
Egypt hopes the forum will launch a broader dialogue on African cities and economies, the future of their infrastructure, and ways to build a more connected continent with greater capacity for production, manufacturing, and trade, he added.
Madbouly said New Alamein’s location on the Mediterranean also underlines Africa’s place at the heart of global trade and investment flows.
He said the continent possesses vast natural resources, a large market, one of the world’s youngest populations, and major opportunities in manufacturing, energy, agriculture, technology, services, and the digital economy.
Madbouly acknowledged the challenges facing African development, including access to financing, infrastructure gaps, high capital costs, weak links between markets, and barriers restricting intra-African trade and investment.
He said the key question is no longer what resources and opportunities Africa possesses, but how to transform them into economic and development value.
“How can we move from identifying opportunities to developing projects? From setting priorities to securing financing? And from dialogue to implementation?” he said, according to the Cabinet statement.
Madbouly said Africa needs platforms that bring decision-makers, investors, financial institutions, implementing companies, and development institutions together to tackle obstacles to projects, reduce risks, mobilize financing, and establish partnerships.
Madbouly said Africa has chosen, through Agenda 2063, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and other continental frameworks, to pursue greater economic integration, expand intra-African trade, and develop shared infrastructure.
Achieving those goals requires the private sector to be a genuine partner in designing and implementing solutions, he said.
Governments establish policies and the necessary regulatory environment, while financial and development institutions provide financing and risk-mitigation tools. The private sector, meanwhile, drives investment, innovation, production, trade, and job creation, Madbouly said.
He said Egypt hopes the forum will provide a platform for the African and international business communities to raise challenges facing investors and companies in African markets and discuss ways to strengthen public-private partnerships.
Madbouly also expressed hope that meetings between governments and companies, as well as among businesses themselves, would produce partnerships extending beyond the forum.
The forum is being organised in cooperation with the Egyptian government, the African Union Commission, the African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD), and the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank).
Madbouly said their participation reflects the need for governments, continental institutions, financial institutions, and businesses to work together to advance development.
The forum is taking place alongside other high-level African events hosted by Egypt in New Alamein, including a summit of AUDA-NEPAD’s founding states and the African Union Mid-Year Coordination Meeting.
Madbouly said Egypt views the forum as a culmination of its efforts to support African development and economic integration, including President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi’s chairmanship of AUDA-NEPAD’s Heads of State and Government Orientation Committee from February 2023 to February 2026.
He said Egypt used its chairmanship to support continental priorities and projects and promote practical solutions to financing and implementation challenges.
Madbouly said the forum comes as rapid economic and technological changes reshape global supply chains, production centres, trade, and investment.
These changes require Africa to be seen not only through its development challenges but also as a continent offering significant opportunities and capable of playing an active role in the changing global economy, he said.
Madbouly called for joint efforts to transform opportunities into investment, investment into industries, and industries into jobs and growth for African peoples.
He concluded by welcoming participants and thanking the AU Commission, AUDA-NEPAD, Afreximbank, and other partners involved in organizing the forum.
The Alamein-Africa Forum brings together ministers, officials, business leaders, and private-sector representatives from Egypt and other African countries, alongside African and international financial and development institutions.

AfDB and German Ministry Partner to Advance Africa Railway Integration
The African Development Bank Group and the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development have entered a partnership aimed at developing Africa's railway systems and deepening regional economic integration, according to MiningWeekly.com. The two organisations will work together to lower transport costs across the continent, improve cross-border interoperability, encourage low-carbon transport solutions and promote sustainable transport policies.
The collaboration also targets the creation of a strong local labour market in the railway sector, pursued through skills transfer, vocational training and the generation of sustainable employment opportunities.
The partnership will begin with a joint feasibility study for an African Rail Competence Centre. The study is to be carried out by the German development cooperation organisation GIZ and is expected to launch this month, with the aim of bringing together innovation and training to modernise and expand the continent's railways.
Africa's rail network currently accounts for only 8% to 10% of the global total, while the African Continental Free Trade Area is driving rising demand for cross-border freight and passenger movement across a market of more than 1.4-billion people.
AfDB Group Infrastructure and Urban Development director Mike Salawou outlined five priorities for the sector: a continental market driven by the AfCFTA, modal-shift reforms, interoperable standards, financing that crowds in private capital, and the competencies required to operate networks once they are built.
Salawou indicated that African governments and railway authorities should establish a clear vision, commission credible feasibility studies, reform early and provide investors with regulatory certainty. He added that European industry should offer long-term partnership, local content and skills transfer rather than only equipment.
He also said financiers should engage in projects at the preparation stage, with the AfDB supporting them through guarantees, blended finance and technical assistance.
The bank backs investments in the Lobito Corridor, the Standard Gauge Railway programme in East Africa, the Nacala Corridor, Algeria's North-South Rail Corridor, Morocco's high-speed rail system and urban rail projects in Senegal and Nigeria.
BMZ economic cooperation deputy director-general Michael Krake said the ministry is working with African partners to strengthen regional connectivity and support sustainable economic development, and that cooperation with the AfDB will advance practical work on interoperability, skills development and other priorities for a stronger railway sector.

articles.full_text:
A boardroom acronym for four emerging markets has grown into something far bigger. Today It is a geopolitical bloc spanning four continents. The journey runs from a four-country dialogue to today's far wider grouping. Successive waves of membership pulled in oil states, African economies and Southeast Asian partners. At the centre of this expanding architecture sits India this year, chairing the grouping for a fourth time since its inception.
BRICS: Shaping an Inclusive Global Order
BRICS has emerged as a key platform for coordinating economic policy among major emerging economies. It serves as the principal forum where these nations shape a common position on global governance. Through sustained dialogue, it has become a channel for advancing the interests of the Global South within multilateral institutions. Its agenda spans development, finance, technology, trade and people-to-people exchanges. The grouping reflects the growing economic weight and aspirations of emerging economies globally. It provides members with a platform to share experiences and address common challenges.
Under its 2026 Presidency, India is set to host the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026. It will mark India’s fourth Chairship of BRICS in 2026. India’s Chairship is guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.” The theme reflects India’s focus on strengthening existing achievements and institutional effectiveness. It places development, sustainability and innovation at the heart of the agenda. It also highlights the aspirations of the Global South. India seeks to reinforce BRICS as a constructive and solutions-oriented forum.
Today, BRICS comprises 11 countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE. Collectively, these members represent 49.5% of the global population, 40% of global GDP, and 26% of global trade. These figures underline their substantial demographic and economic weight. Its expanded membership has also widened its geographical reach across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America. This diversity brings together major markets, natural resources, technological capabilities and varied development experiences.
| The Origin The acronym ‘BRIC’ was coined in 2001 by Goldman Sachs in its Global Economics Paper, ‘The World Needs Better Economic BRICs.’ Based on econometric analysis, the paper projected that Brazil, Russia, India and China would be among the world’s largest economies over the following five decades. Their growing economic weight and vast geographic reach across three continents highlighted their emerging global significance. The BRIC concept subsequently evolved into a formal grouping, with South Africa joining in 2010 and transforming BRIC into BRICS. The evolution marked the transition from an economic grouping identified by analysts to a formal platform for political, economic and development cooperation. | 
The Aim, Objective and Areas of Cooperation
BRICS was initially conceived as a forum for dialogue on major issues shaping the international agenda. Its early focus was on developing common positions on global political and economic matters. It sought to promote a more democratic, legitimate and balanced international order. The grouping also emphasised sustainable economic and social development, social inclusion and shared prosperity among emerging economies. Over time, these priorities have provided a foundation for deeper and broader engagement among members.
Across successive summits, BRICS cooperation has progressively expanded to encompass strategic global issues and areas of practical collaboration. Its agenda covers terrorism, climate change, food and energy security, trade and agriculture. It also addresses labour and employment, telecommunications, international finance and the global economic situation. BRICS advocates for greater representation and equity in international institutions, including the WTO and global financial architecture. These efforts seek to make global governance more inclusive, effective and responsive to contemporary challenges.
BRICS Through the Years: From Crisis to Collective Action
The 2008 global financial crisis marked a defining moment in the evolution of BRICS. It exposed gaps in the existing global financial architecture. It also created a need for broader consensus on global economic governance. The four BRIC countries articulated a common position on these issues. They called for a more representative international financial system. They sought greater voice for emerging economies in the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. They also opposed protectionism and supported an open, rules-based multilateral trading system. This coordination laid the foundation for the first BRIC Summit in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009.
BRIC was formally established in 2006 as a political cooperation forum among Brazil, Russia, India and China. Its founding members shared an aspiration for a more representative and equitable global order. South Africa joined as a full member in 2011, transforming BRIC into BRICS. This inclusion expanded the grouping’s geographical representation across continents. The grouping subsequently broadened its agenda beyond economic issues to development, finance, health, climate action, technology and trade. This evolution strengthened BRICS as a wider framework for engagement among emerging economies.
A Wider BRICS: Expanding Reach, Deepening Engagement
A major phase of expansion began in January 2024. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE became full members. Indonesia joined as the eleventh full member in January 2025. These accessions significantly expanded BRICS’ geographical and economic reach. The expansion was accompanied by the creation of a Partner Country category. Ten countries joined this framework during 2025: Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam. The new arrangement provides an additional channel for structured engagement with BRICS.
The Partner Country framework broadens BRICS’ outreach without altering its full-membership structure. It strengthens opportunities for South-South cooperation across Asia, Africa, Latin America and Eurasia. The wider network also creates scope for collaboration on trade, finance, climate action and sustainable development. It reflects growing interest among emerging economies in participating in discussions on global governance.
The evolution of BRICS demonstrates a shift from a four-country economic dialogue to a broader framework for political, economic, financial and social cooperation. Its expansion has increased its demographic and economic weight. It has also broadened its regional representation and areas of engagement. The grouping’s institutional evolution has kept pace with the changing priorities of emerging economies.
| BRICS Presidency: Rotation and Responsibilities The BRICS Presidency rotates annually according to the letters of its acronym. Each Presidency term begins on January 1st and concludes on December 31st of the respective year. The country holding the Presidency sets the priorities of the agenda for that year. It also organizes the group's annual Summit and steers key ministerial and working group meetings. With the recent expansion of BRICS membership, a new rotation formula for the Presidency is also being discussed among member countries. | 
India at the Helm of BRICS: From Continuity to Consensus
Before this year, India has previously chaired BRICS in 2012, 2016 and 2021. Each Chairship reflected the priorities and challenges of its respective period. India’s repeated leadership demonstrates its sustained engagement with the grouping. It also reflects India’s commitment to constructive multilateralism and the priorities of developing economies.
2012: Laying the Foundation for Stronger Cooperation
India hosted the Fourth BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 29 March 2012. The Summit was held under the theme “BRICS Partnership for Global Stability, Security and Prosperity.” Discussions focused on global governance reform, sustainable development, food security and energy security. The Summit adopted the Delhi Declaration and an Action Plan for strengthening BRICS cooperation. The outcomes established a stronger foundation for institutional and sectoral engagement. Click to Read More About the Delhi Declaration
| Major Outcomes | 
2016: Goa Summit Expanded BRICS Outreach
India hosted the Eighth BRICS Summit in Goa in October 2016. The Summit was held under the theme “Building Responsive, Inclusive and Collective Solutions.” India’s Chairship focused on strengthening intra-BRICS cooperation and expanding outreach. It also advanced collaboration on counter-terrorism, trade, innovation and multilateral coordination. The Goa Summit reinforced the grouping’s focus on emerging global challenges and practical cooperation.
| Major Outcome | 
2021: Consolidating Cooperation in a Changing World
India hosted the 13th BRICS Summit virtually on 9 September 2021. The Summit marked the 15th anniversary of BRICS. It was held under the theme “BRICS@15: Intra-BRICS Cooperation for Continuity, Consolidation and Consensus.” India focused on strengthening institutional continuity, deepening cooperation and building greater consensus. The Chairship also advanced cooperation across health, digital technologies, counter-terrorism and sustainable development.
Through successive Chairships, India has contributed to the institutional and substantive development of BRICS. Its priorities have evolved with emerging global challenges while retaining a focus on practical cooperation. India’s 2026 Chairship builds on this experience and the grouping’s expanded membership.
